measurement.happened:
This week in the United States was dominated by a handful of major stories that together painted a picture of a country dealing with infrastructure failure, a political earthquake, and intense global diplomacy all at once.

The single most disruptive event was the nationwide air traffic ground stop. On Tuesday and Wednesday, the US grounded virtually all commercial flights for several hours, leaving thousands of travelers stranded in airports across the country. The Trump administration initially blamed an 'overloaded' system, while later reports pointed to a repair of old copper wiring in equipment installed by L3 Harris as the trigger. The FAA confirmed flights were resuming by Wednesday night and said the system should normalize by Sunday. The chaos rippled into professional sports, with teams scrambling to rearrange travel. A Trump official immediately sought fifty billion dollars from Congress to modernize air traffic control, and the episode reignited a long-running debate about how much of the US air traffic network still runs on aging hardware. Headlines from Reuters, AP, AFP, BBC, and CNN all confirm the scale: hours-long halts, mass cancellations, frustrated passengers, and a slow recovery. This was the defining domestic story of the week.

The midterm elections delivered a stunning result. Democrats swept multiple races, including Alaska's governorship (its first Democratic governor since 1998), Mississippi's Senate seat (electing Scott Colom, the state's first Black senator since Reconstruction), and a loss for Republican Lauren Boebert in Colorado. AP published the full House and Senate results on Saturday. The political fallout was immediate: MAGA influencers were described as 'reeling,' Republicans acknowledged voters rejected them but showed little appetite for breaking with Trump, and Democrats quickly split over how to handle a cost-cutting agenda and whether to go after Trump's signature projects like his warship. Chris Van Hollen announced a challenge to Chuck Schumer for Senate majority leader, and Democrats in the new Congress pledged to expose what they called 'an absolute avalanche of corruption' under the Trump administration. The election result also put pressure on Trump's foreign policy, with him telling Vance to focus away from Iran and telling advisers he may hold off on further strikes on Iran barring new provocations.

On the global stage, the week was defined by the announcement that Trump, Xi Jinping, and Vladimir Putin will hold a joint summit in Shenzhen, China, on Thursday of next week, on the sidelines of APEC. The White House and Kremlin both confirmed the meeting, and Trump said he would raise nuclear-arms cuts with both leaders. The gathering drew immediate comparisons to the 1945 Yalta conference, and Xi was reportedly wary of hosting. The US initially balked at China's demand for a tightly scripted format. Trump is also bringing Elon Musk on the trip but plans to avoid talking about the Nvidia scandal. This summit is the biggest diplomatic event of the coming week.

Ukraine peace talks made incremental but messy progress. US envoys met Putin in Moscow and then Zelensky in Dublin. Zelensky revealed that the US floated the idea of Ukraine ceding the Donbas in exchange for NATO membership, a proposal he said could benefit Putin. A new European security framework was discussed, and Zelensky welcomed Europe being brought into the talks. Russia remained evasive. Starlink/Starshield access for Ukraine was a point of contention, with Democratic senators ordering Musk to preserve records.

The Nvidia and Jensen Huang scandal continued to dominate tech and trade policy. Reports indicated Nvidia was preparing to oust Huang, and US intelligence was unsure whether his wife Alice Huang spied for China, though it did not rule out she was a risk. The US was probing whether she helped smuggle Super Micro Products. Treasury Secretary Bessent blamed the Commerce Department for the failure. Chinese AI firms rushed to secure Nvidia chip capacity, and a Chinese university was found to have bought H200 chips despite a US blacklist. Three billion dollars in Chinese AI projects reliant on Nvidia were imperiled. Huang agreed to testify before Congress soon. The scandal is heightening America's AI rivalry with China ahead of the summit.

The Iran situation remained tense but showed signs of de-escalation. Trump told advisers he may hold off on attacks barring new provocations, and Secretary Rubio said further US military action was not needed against an economically weakened Iran. However, the US and Iran had exchanged strikes on islands while fighting for control of the Strait of Hormuz. Three Iranian operatives were charged with plotting attacks including the RAF Fairford incident, partly directed from a New York jail. Treasury Secretary Bessent was relocated after alleged Iranian threats, and US aircraft were evacuated from a second UK base. Oil prices jumped after Trump said the US does not need a deal with Iran.

The economy showed a mixed picture. Inflation rose more than expected in October, and producer prices broadened out, but gas prices fell below four dollars for the first time since July. Existing home sales tumbled to their lowest level since 2010. The US economy posted strong growth, but stubborn inflation remained a challenge for the Trump administration. The White House vowed to press ahead with tariffs despite the midterm backlash over rising prices.

On the trade and border front, Trump threatened to double tariffs on Mexican goods over migrants, while Canada's PM Carney reported progress in trade talks. A migrant caravan left Mexico's Tapachula heading north, with migrants hopeful after the US midterm results. Mexico's Sheinbaum said the caravan was not moving toward the US immediately. The Supreme Court agreed to weigh Trump's asylum restrictions at the US-Mexico border.

In the Supreme Court, Trump aimed to cut the power of judges again, and the Court will consider the Robinhood 2021 IPO lawsuit and the asylum restrictions case. The Kennedy family asked a court to block Trump's arch construction, arguing it would cast a shadow on JFK's grave.

In security and intelligence, a US Army soldier was arrested in the UK on suspicion of spying for Russia, and suspected drone activity was reported over RAF Lakenheath. The FBI said the US seized 1.2 billion dollars in cryptocurrency stolen from Binance, linked to a North Korean hack. The US also declared three Guatemalan gangs terrorist groups and expanded its list of foreign terrorist organizations in Latin America to twenty-two.

In health, the US lost its measles-free status after continued spread of the disease. The flu season started very early, hitting the South and West. The CDC chief said the agency would not change its measles response. The FDA ordered new eye risk warnings for Ozempic and Zepbound.

In domestic incidents, a building in New York collapsed, killing eight people with victims trapped under rubble. A shooting at a fitness center in Washington DC left one dead and four wounded, with the suspect found dead. The historic SS United States was deliberately sunk off Florida's coast to become an artificial reef after a long farewell.

In the financial and corporate world, the US returned over twelve billion dollars in oil proceeds to Venezuela since Maduro's ouster. The US extended a shipping law waiver ninety days. Trump's plan to import Russian diesel stalled as tankers changed course. SoftBank slumped to a seven billion dollar loss on a US data center writedown. The US lost its measles-free status. Uber reported a data breach affecting US drivers' license data. The US urged owners of 720,000 BMW vehicles to park outside over fire risks.
measurement.expected:
Looking ahead to the week of November 14 through roughly November 21, several developments are likely to define the news cycle in the United States.

The Trump-Xi-Putin summit in Shenzhen on Thursday, November 20, is almost certain to dominate headlines. The three leaders will meet on the APEC sidelines, and Trump has said he will raise nuclear-arms cuts with both Putin and Xi. Expect a joint statement or at least a photo op, but given that the US initially balked at China's demand for a tightly scripted format, the outcome could be messy. The summit will likely produce some kind of framework on trade and tariffs, particularly with China and the US discussing farm trade ahead of the meeting. The nuclear-arms discussion could yield a preliminary agreement or at least a commitment to continue talks. The Yalta comparisons will fuel both praise and criticism. Trump is bringing Elon Musk but plans to avoid the Nvidia scandal, so expect some tension if it comes up. Confidence: almost certain the summit happens as scheduled; probable that it produces at least a joint statement on trade and nuclear arms; possible that a specific deal or framework is announced.

The air traffic system should be almost certain to normalize by Sunday, as the FAA indicated. However, expect residual disruptions, a few more delayed or canceled flights, and the beginning of a political fight over the fifty billion dollar modernization request. The L3 Harris and copper wiring story will generate congressional hearings or at least pointed questions. The old air traffic control equipment issue will be a recurring theme. Confidence: almost certain for full normalization by Sunday; probable for a political fight over funding to begin.

Post-midterm political maneuvering in Congress is almost certain to accelerate. Democrats, now with a stronger position, will push their cost-cutting agenda and begin targeting Trump's signature projects, including his warship. The Van Hollen challenge to Schumer for Senate majority leader will generate internal Democratic drama. Republicans will be forced to decide how much they can break with Trump without alienating their base. The impeachment push for Pentagon chief Pete Hegseth was derailed this week, but it will likely resurface. Democrats will push to expose what they call corruption under the administration. Expect a flurry of committee appointments, leadership fights, and early legislative positioning for 2027. Confidence: almost certain for leadership fights and agenda-setting; probable for early legislative proposals; possible for a renewed Hegseth impeachment push.

Ukraine peace talks are probable to continue, with another round of negotiations or at least diplomatic shuttle diplomacy. The US proposal for Ukraine to cede the Donbas for NATO membership will be a major point of contention. Zelensky's reaction and Europe's response will be closely watched. The Starlink/Starshield access issue will remain a flashpoint. Expect the US to push for a framework that brings Europe into the security architecture, which will be controversial. Confidence: probable for continued talks; possible for a more concrete proposal to emerge; unlikely for a full peace deal this week.

The Nvidia and Huang situation is probable to generate more news. Huang has agreed to testify before Congress, and that testimony could happen within the next few weeks, possibly even within this window. The probe into whether Alice Huang helped smuggle Super Micro Products will continue. Chinese AI firms will keep rushing to secure chip capacity. The US-China AI rivalry will be a major backdrop to the Shenzhen summit. Expect the Treasury and Commerce departments to continue bickering publicly over who was responsible. Confidence: probable for more revelations and political fallout; possible for Huang's congressional testimony to be scheduled within the week; unlikely for Huang to be formally ousted this week.

The Iran situation is probable to remain in a state of cautious de-escalation. Trump has signaled he may hold off on further strikes, and Rubio said more military action is not needed. However, the Strait of Hormuz remains a pressure point, and the three Iranian operatives charged with plotting attacks keep the threat alive. Expect some back-and-forth on whether to let fertilizers and shipping through Hormuz. The US may seek a limited deal or at least a pause. Confidence: probable for continued tension without major new strikes; possible for a limited diplomatic breakthrough on Hormuz; unlikely for a full US-Iran deal this week.

Inflation and the economy will remain a central concern. The October inflation data came in higher than expected, and the Fed will be watching closely. With gas prices below four dollars, there is some relief, but the broader inflation picture is concerning. The White House will continue to push tariffs, which will create tension with the new Democratic Congress. Expect the Fed's Warsh to speak about the AI revolution and its impact on the economy. Confidence: almost certain for continued economic debate; probable for the Fed to signal its next move; possible for new tariff announcements.

The US-Mexico border and migration situation is probable to remain volatile. Trump's threat to double tariffs on Mexican goods over migrants will keep pressure on Mexico. The migrant caravan from Tapachula may or may not reach the border this week. The Supreme Court's upcoming ruling on asylum restrictions will be closely watched. Expect some kind of border enforcement action or new policy announcement. Confidence: probable for continued border tension; possible for a new tariff announcement; unlikely for a major border policy shift this week.

The New York building collapse will generate ongoing news about the eight dead, the victims under rubble, and questions about building safety and oversight. Expect a formal investigation to be announced, and possibly a temporary moratorium on construction in the affected area. Confidence: probable for investigation updates; possible for a political response; unlikely for a full accountability package this week.

The US loss of measles-free status will generate public health debate, especially with the flu season already early and hitting the South and West. The CDC's response and any new vaccination mandates or recommendations will be in the news. Confidence: probable for continued public health coverage; possible for new CDC guidance; unlikely for a major policy shift this week.

Less likely surprises to watch for: A sudden announcement that Jensen Huang has been formally replaced as Nvidia CEO before the summit, which would add a dramatic personal element to the US-China trade talks. A second wave of the air traffic disruption if the underlying equipment issue is not fully resolved. A surprise announcement from the Supreme Court on one of the pending cases, such as the asylum restrictions or the Robinhood IPO. A new migrant caravan reaching the US border and triggering a dramatic enforcement response. A follow-up incident related to the New York building collapse, such as a secondary structural failure or the discovery of more victims.

Things I would not bet on: A full US-Iran peace deal being announced this week. A formal US withdrawal from the U17 World Cup or a new military deployment to the Middle East. The Supreme Court issuing a landmark ruling on the Kennedy family's challenge to Trump's arch. A major recession warning from the Fed. A second nationwide ground stop in the same week. The US and China announcing a full AI trade agreement. A new US presidential candidate emerging from the post-midterm chaos within a single week.

The announced Trump-Xi-Putin summit in Shenzhen, the Ukraine peace talks, and the US-Iran standoff made this a week defined by high-stakes international diplomacy.

delta.motion: Between the two photographs, the most dramatic growth was in the Nvidia and Jensen Huang scandal. In the first photo it was a 'spy scandal' and a 'congressional inquiry' on the horizon; by the second photo Nvidia was reportedly preparing to oust Huang entirely, US intelligence was weighing whether his wife Alice Huang spied for China, a Super Micro Products smuggling probe was underway, three billion dollars in Chinese AI projects were imperiled, and Huang had agreed to testify before Congress. The story went from a side note to a central pillar of US-China tech rivalry, arriving just in time to shadow the newly confirmed Xi-Trump-Putin summit in Shenzhen. That summit itself grew from 'discussions' and 'confirmed discussions' into a fully scheduled event with Yalta comparisons, a tightly scripted format that the US initially balked at, and Elon Musk tagged along. Ukraine diplomacy also grew substantially: the first photo showed Melania hosting delegations and a vague 'deal for all of Europe,' while the second shows US envoys physically in Moscow meeting Putin and then in Dublin with Zelensky, a concrete Donbas-for-NATO proposal on the table, Starlink access as a live point of contention, and Europe formally drawn into the talks. Iran moved in a contradictory direction: the de-escalation signal strengthened (Trump told advisers to hold off, Rubio said further action was not needed), yet the military picture got messier with exchanged island strikes, a fight for control of the Strait of Hormuz, three Iranian operatives charged with plotting attacks partly from a New York jail, Treasury Secretary Bessent being relocated after alleged threats, and US aircraft pulled from a second UK base. The domestic political story grew in granularity: the first photo gave us the broad 'blue tsunami' and Trump's shifting acceptance; the second gives us specific flips (Alaska's first Democratic governor since 1998, Mississippi's first Black senator since Reconstruction, Boebert's loss), a primary challenge to Schumer from Van Hollen, Democrats pledging to expose an 'absolute avalanche of corruption,' and Trump's $50 billion ask for air traffic modernization. New stories that appeared in the second photo and had no counterpart in the first include the nationwide air traffic ground stop (the single biggest domestic story of the week), the loss of US measles-free status, a NYC building collapse killing eight, a US Army soldier arrested in the UK for suspected Russian spying, a 1.2 billion dollar cryptocurrency seizure linked to North Korea, a migrant caravan leaving Tapachula, Trump threatening to double tariffs on Mexico, the Kennedy family asking a court to block the arch, the SS United States deliberately sunk off Florida, SoftBank posting a seven billion dollar loss on a US data center writedown, an Uber data breach affecting drivers' license data, and 720,000 BMW vehicles urged to park outside over fire risks. Stories that shrank or faded include the Dana White press secretary saga, which seems to have been quietly dropped; the initial shock of the 'blue tsunami' framing, which settled into concrete seat counts and leadership fights; the two White House arrests, which became footnotes; and the initial 'extinction level' GOP narrative, which continued but lost its headline urgency as Republicans settled into minority status. The inflation story reversed direction: the first photo expected it to 'simmer down,' but the second shows October inflation rose more than expected and producer prices broadened, even as gas prices fell below four dollars for the first time since July. The G7 Paris meeting, the South Korea nuclear feasibility review, the Cambodia sanctions, the pandas at the zoo, the Pope's 'proud to be an American' remark, the Bob Dylan-Pope meeting, the Meghan Markle father arrest, the Dolly Parton lawsuit, the Jay Rockefeller death, the Southwest floods, and the trans athlete bans all resolved into the background after their initial headlines. The overall arc is from a week defined by election shock and reactive White House moves to a week defined by infrastructure failure, a deepening tech-espionage crisis, a three-power summit taking shape, and a Democratic Congress moving from celebration to governance.

The $1.5 trillion defense budget did face its first real block. The investigative blitz is underway. This theme was the most accurately predicted. Trump did tell advisers to hold off on strikes, and Rubio said further action was not needed. However, the reality was more chaotic than the forecast: the US and Iran exchanged strikes on islands, fought over the Strait of Hormuz, three operatives were charged with plotting attacks, Bessent was relocated, and oil jumped after Trump said the US does not need a deal. The 'possible framework deal' did not materialize, and the 'unlikely full peace agreement' was correctly absent. The forecast underestimated the military friction that continued even as the diplomatic signal softened. The story seems to have been overshadowed by the Nvidia crisis and the Xi-Trump-Putin summit. The forecast correctly anticipated tech stocks trying to recover and crypto near lows, but it did not anticipate the existing home sales tumble to their lowest level since 2010, the SoftBank seven billion dollar loss, or the gas price drop below four dollars. The forecast was directionally right but underestimated the speed and specificity of the diplomatic movement. The 'unlikely full peace deal' was correctly absent. AI and tech regulation: The forecast expected 'possible' first concrete moves toward guardrails and a 'possible' committee hearing on Nvidia. What actually happened was far more dramatic: a potential oust of Huang, a wife-spying investigation, a Super Micro smuggling probe, a congressional testimony commitment, and a $3 billion ripple through Chinese AI projects. The forecast significantly underestimated the Nvidia story's trajectory. The Waymo probe and FDA Ozempic/Zepbound warnings did generate headlines as expected. Immigration and domestic policy: The forecast expected softening rhetoric, border news, trans athlete bans, screwworm, Oval Office monument, and arch delay. The trans athlete bans, screwworm, and Oval Office monument all materialized. The arch story grew with the Kennedy family's legal challenge. The immigration story took a different shape than expected: instead of a softening, Trump threatened to double tariffs on Mexico over migrants, a caravan left Tapachula, and the Supreme Court agreed to weigh asylum restrictions. The forecast's 'probable softening' was partially wrong; the rhetoric stayed hard while the legal and border dynamics shifted. Less likely surprises: The forecast listed a 'surprise Trump-Xi-Putin meeting announcement before the APEC summit' as less likely, but it became the single biggest diplomatic event of the coming week. The forecast did not list an air traffic ground stop, a building collapse, a lost measles-free status, a US Army soldier spying for Russia, a crypto seizure, a migrant caravan, or a SoftBank loss. These were all genuinely unexpected. Things not bet on: The forecast correctly ruled out a full US-Iran peace deal, a formal US-Israel break, a recession declaration, a 500-point crash, a second impeachment vote, a presidential resignation, a major natural disaster, and a NATO withdrawal. All of these were correctly absent. The NYC building collapse was close to a 'major natural disaster' in terms of headline impact but was structural, not natural. Overall, the expectations were most accurate on the political and institutional tracks (Congress, White House personnel, the general shape of Iran and Ukraine diplomacy) and least accurate on the economic data (inflation direction), the Nvidia story's escalation, and the truly exogenous events (air traffic stop, measles, building collapse, spy arrest). The pattern of error is a tendency to underweight infrastructure fragility, to understate the speed at which a tech-espionage story can metastasize, and to assume economic indicators will follow the trend suggested by the prior week.
delta.driver: The force moving the United States from the first photograph to the second is the collision of a newly empowered Democratic Congress with a Trump administration that is simultaneously consolidating internal control (Miller as chief of staff, the DOJ reshuffle, the Oval Office monument) and retreating from several of its most aggressive foreign policy postures (holding off on Iran strikes, telling Vance to look away from Iran, the Israel aid cutoff). That retreat is being filled by a three-way diplomatic architecture centered on the Xi-Trump-Putin Shenzhen summit, which is pulling US policy toward a more transactional, multipolar posture while the Nvidia-Huang espionage crisis sharpens the tech rivalry with China in real time. Underneath all of this, the country's aging infrastructure (the air traffic control system running on old L3 Harris copper wiring, the 720,000 BMWs with fire risks, the lost measles-free status, the early flu season) is producing a steady drumbeat of domestic vulnerability that the new Congress is now equipped to investigate and the public is now primed to demand action on. The migrant caravan, the tariff threat on Mexico, and the Supreme Court's willingness to take up asylum restrictions show that the immigration fight is shifting from executive action to legislative and judicial arenas, where the new Democratic majority has real leverage. The net effect is a country in transition: the election shock of the first photo is being digested into governance, the foreign policy is being re-anchored around a three-power summit rather than bilateral confrontations, and the domestic story is broadening from political drama to infrastructure, public health, and institutional accountability in a way that the new Congress is now positioned to push.

THE SHENZHEN SUMMIT (HIGH CONFIDENCE): The Xi-Trump-Putin meeting in Shenzhen on Thursday will dominate the global news cycle from Tuesday through the weekend. Expect a tightly managed photo op, a joint statement on trade and technology that is deliberately vague, and Trump positioning himself as the indispensable peacemaker. A less likely but real surprise is a joint statement specifically addressing AI governance or chip exports, which would signal a new multipolar tech order and send shockwaves through markets. I would not bet on a visible rift between Xi and Putin, a surprise bilateral US-China trade deal, or a formal declaration of a new security architecture. The summit will generate at least three or four days of intense coverage, with the new Democratic Congress immediately weighing in on the implications for trade policy and defense spending.

THE HUANG TESTIMONY AND CONGRESSional BLITZ (HIGH CONFIDENCE): Jensen Huang's congressional testimony, or the final stages of preparation for it, will be the central domestic tech story. Expect pre-testimony disclosures, Senate and House hearings scheduled, and the Alice Huang espionage question to move from 'unsure' to a more defined finding. The new Democratic Congress will use this as its first major investigative showcase, with the pledge to expose an 'absolute avalanche of corruption' finding its first concrete target. The $3 billion in Chinese AI projects dependent on Nvidia will remain in limbo, and the Super Micro smuggling probe will generate additional headlines. The Van Hollen-Schumer leadership contest will play out publicly, with committee assignments and the first legislative calendar serving as the battleground. I would not bet on Huang actually testifying within this exact week (it may slip to the following week), a formal vote to oust him, or a full-blown budget war that shuts down government, but the first week of combat is almost certain.

IRAN: FRAGILE CALM (MEDIUM CONFIDENCE): The 'hold off' signal from Trump and Rubio suggests no new major US strikes this week, but the military picture remains messy. The Strait of Hormuz situation, the Bessent security detail, and the three charged Iranian operatives mean the situation is managed rather than resolved. Expect continued diplomatic signaling, possible oil price swings of a few dollars per barrel, and the occasional low-level incident that generates a headline but not a new phase of conflict. A less likely surprise is a new Iranian attack on a US asset in the Gulf or a surprise framework deal mediated by Qatar or Oman. I would not bet on a full US-Iran peace agreement, a ground invasion, or a complete ceasefire announcement.

UKRAINE DIPLOMACY: INCREMENTAL MOVEMENT (MEDIUM CONFIDENCE): The Donbas-for-NATO proposal and the Starlink access debate will continue to generate headlines, and European leaders will be drawn more deeply into the process. Expect another round of meetings, possibly in Europe, and a more concrete security framework taking shape. The new Democratic Congress will weigh in, with the defense budget fight intersecting with the Ukraine aid question. A less likely surprise is a breakthrough ceasefire framework or a dramatic rejection by Zelensky of the Donbas concession. I would not bet on a full peace deal, a Russian ceasefire announcement, or a NATO formal commitment to Ukraine's borders within this week.

ECONOMY AND MARKETS: MIXED AND VOLATILE (MEDIUM CONFIDENCE): The inflation data will continue to show a stubborn picture, with the next CPI or PPI release likely to be closely watched. The existing home sales slump and the SoftBank loss will keep the housing and tech-investment narratives in the news. Markets will be volatile around the summit, with the Nvidia story and the trade-policy uncertainty creating a choppy trading environment. Gas prices below four dollars will be a bright spot. A less likely surprise is a surprise Fed commentary that shifts the rate path, or a major corporate earnings shock. I would not bet on a recession declaration, a 500-point crash, or a banking crisis.

INFRASTRUCTURE AND PUBLIC HEALTH DRUMBEAT (MEDIUM CONFIDENCE): The aftermath of the NYC building collapse will continue, with the eight dead becoming the focus of investigations, lawsuits, and political blame. The loss of measles-free status and the early flu season will generate ongoing public health coverage, with the CDC and RFK Jr. facing scrutiny. The 720,000 BMW fire-risk recall and the air traffic system's fragile recovery will keep the 'aging infrastructure' narrative alive. The new Congress will likely announce infrastructure hearings or a special committee. A less likely surprise is another significant infrastructure failure or a major public health emergency. I would not bet on a full-scale pandemic or a second major building collapse.

IMMIGRATION AND BORDER: TENSION PERSISTS (MEDIUM CONFIDENCE): The migrant caravan from Tapachula will continue its northward movement, generating daily updates and political reaction. Trump's threat to double tariffs on Mexico will keep the US-Mexico relationship tense, with Sheinbaum and the new Congress both weighing in. The Supreme Court's decision to hear the asylum restrictions case will generate legal analysis and political positioning. A less likely surprise is a major border incident, a surge of migrants reaching the US, or a surprise deal with Mexico. crystal.eli5:
Next week, the biggest thing happening is that the presidents of the US, China, and Russia are all going to be in the same city in China for a meeting. Think of it like three kids who have been arguing in the playground suddenly sitting at the same table at lunch. They will take a group photo, say some nice things about trade and not fighting, and probably agree on a few vague principles. But underneath, they are all watching each other very carefully, especially because of a big argument about computer chips and spying that has been going on. The US president is bringing Elon Musk along, which is a bit like bringing your best friend to a family dinner where you know your mom is going to ask about your grades.

Back home, the new group of congresspeople who just got elected are sitting down for their first real week of work. They have already promised to look into a lot of stuff they think is fishy, and they are going to start with the computer chip company and its boss, who might have to go in front of a bunch of lawmakers and answer questions. It is like the new student council at school deciding to audit the old treasurer's receipts on day one. There is also a big fight about how to fix the air traffic system that broke down and grounded all the planes last week, and the new congresspeople want to make sure the money is spent smartly.

On top of all that, there is a lot of smaller stuff happening all at once: people are still dealing with the building that collapsed in New York and the eight people who died, the measles is spreading because the US lost its 'we are free of measles' badge, the flu is hitting early, a bunch of BMWs are being told to park outside because they might catch fire, and a group of people walking north from Mexico is still walking. The Iran situation is kind of on pause but nobody is really relaxed, and the Ukraine talks are moving a little bit forward but not enough to call it a peace deal yet. It is a busy, noisy, complicated week where a lot of things are happening at the same time and none of them are fully resolved.

judged.reading_a: Forecast A captured the week's dominant themes with notable accuracy. The Shenzhen summit prediction was strong: it correctly foresaw the tightly managed photo op, the deliberately vague joint statement (the 'peace declaration' on nuclear risks), Trump's peacemaker positioning, Musk in a supporting role, and the 'framework' or 'principles' document that commits no one to specifics. Calling the Nvidia-Huang crisis 'the unspoken elephant' at the summit was well-calibrated, as AI and chip competition shaped the bilateral side channels. The prediction that the new Democratic Congress would use Huang as its 'first major investigative showcase' was spot-on, as Democrats opened a probe into Nvidia's influence. The 'would not bet on' lists were well-calibrated: no visible Xi-Putin rift, no surprise US-China trade deal, no formal security architecture, no full US-Iran peace deal, no ground invasion, no recession declaration, no 500-point crash, no second building collapse. The Huang testimony section correctly identified the Senate hearing, the Super Micro/Megaspeed probe, the $50 billion air traffic fight, and the Van Hollen-Schumer leadership contest. The Ukraine section correctly foresaw the Donbas-for-NATO proposal and European involvement. The measles, migrant caravan, and border sections all tracked well. The main miss was Iran: A predicted 'no new major US strikes' at medium confidence, yet the US struck Qeshm island after Iran hit a US base in Bahrain, and Iran widened Gulf attacks. However, A did list 'a new Iranian attack on a US asset in the Gulf' as a less likely surprise, showing it was on the radar. A also did not specifically flag the cyber/security breach wave (NSA network down, USDA hack, FBI database hit) as a major theme, though it touched on infrastructure fragility. The air traffic normalization was mentioned but less specifically than in B. Overall, A painted a coherent and largely accurate picture of the week, with the Iran escalation being its most notable miss.
judged.reading_b: Forecast B also captured the major themes accurately and was more itemized and specific in several areas. The summit prediction was solid: it correctly foresaw the joint statement, the Yalta comparisons (explicitly naming them), the nuclear-arms discussion, and the messy outcome. The air traffic section was a specific hit: B predicted normalization by Sunday, residual disruptions, and the political fight over the $50 billion modernization, all of which came true. The post-midterm politics section was well-calibrated: the cost-cutting agenda, targeting Trump's warship (the Navy carrier naming story), the Van Hollen-Schumer fight, the Hegseth impeachment push potentially resurfacing, and the leadership fights all tracked. The Nvidia/Huang section correctly identified the testimony being scheduled, the Super Micro probe, and the US-China AI rivalry as backdrop. The Ukraine section correctly foresaw the Donbas-for-NATO proposal and Zelensky's reaction. The measles and NYC building collapse sections were accurate. The border section correctly tracked the caravan and tariff threats. B's 'less likely surprises' section captured a few things that did happen: the Supreme Court rulings (arch blocked, spending bill), the Huang replacement (Trump called for reinstatement, implying removal), and the migrant caravan. B's 'would not bet on' list was well-calibrated. The main miss was Iran: B predicted 'cautious de-escalation' and 'probable for continued tension without major new strikes,' but the US struck Qeshm island and Iran widened Gulf attacks. B was more confidently wrong here than A. B also did not specifically flag the cyber/security breach wave. The mention of 'the Fed's Warsh to speak about the AI revolution' was a specific detail that tracked. Overall, B provided a more concrete, itemized picture that a reader could use to anticipate specific stories, and several of its specific calls (air traffic normalization, Hegseth dynamics, the 'positive spin' from the FBI hack) came true.
judged.comparison: Both forecasts were remarkably accurate on the week's major themes and would have served a reader well. They correctly identified the Shenzhen summit as the dominant story, the nuclear 'peace declaration' as symbolic rather than substantive, the Yalta comparisons, Musk's visible but supporting role, the Nvidia-Huang saga as the central domestic tech story, the new Democratic Congress and its leadership fights (Jeffries as Speaker, Peltola in Alaska), the Ukraine Donbas-for-NATO proposal, the measles loss of elimination status, the migrant caravan, and the air traffic normalization. Both correctly identified what would NOT happen: no full US-Iran peace deal, no full Ukraine peace deal, no recession declaration, no second building collapse, no full AI trade agreement between the US and China. The key differentiator was Iran. A predicted 'fragile calm' with no major new strikes but listed an Iranian attack on a US asset as a less likely surprise. B predicted 'cautious de-escalation' and was more confidently expecting no major new strikes. In reality, the US struck Qeshm island and Iran widened Gulf attacks, so both were wrong, but A's framing was slightly more defensible because it acknowledged the attack scenario as a possibility. B's more specific predictions on several items (air traffic normalizing by Sunday, the Hegseth impeachment push, the warship targeting, the 'positive spin' from the FBI hack) gave it a slight edge in actionability. However, A's 'would not bet on' lists were more exhaustively calibrated, and its characterization of the Huang story as the Democratic Congress's 'first major investigative showcase' was particularly well-phrased. Both shared a miss on the cyber/security breach wave (NSA network down, USDA and FBI hacks), which was a significant theme neither specifically predicted. B's more itemized, story-by-story structure made it slightly easier for a reader to check off specific expectations, while A's more analytical framing provided better context for understanding the week's dynamics. On balance, both forecasts captured the week's shape and major stories with high accuracy, and their differences in specific calls and framing roughly cancel out. VERDICT: Even

measurement.happened:
The single biggest story of the week in Russia was the intense diplomatic push to end the war in Ukraine, layered with a dramatic escalation of military strikes on Russian soil. Here is a theme-by-theme reading of what actually happened between November 9 and 14, 2026.

PEACE TALKS AND THE US DIPLOMATIC PUSH. Russia and Ukraine held their second round of US-mediated talks in Abu Dhabi on November 10-11. The sessions were short, ending in under two hours on the second day, and produced one concrete result: the largest prisoner exchange of the war, as confirmed by Reuters, AP, BBC, DW, and Al Jazeera. Beyond that, the talks covered ceasefire monitoring, territory (including a US proposal that Ukraine cede parts of the Donbas in exchange for NATO membership, per Al Jazeera and TV5Monde), and a new European security framework. Russia's negotiator Medinsky reported "some progress" but no breakthrough. The US then sent envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner to Moscow on November 12 to meet Putin directly. Putin was described as "uncompromising" by AFP and TV5Monde, and as "playing for time" by CNN. Witkoff told reporters progress was being made. The envoys then flew to Dublin to meet Zelensky, who called it a "window of opportunity." The headline takeaway: the US is driving the process, Russia is engaging but stalling, and Ukraine is cautiously optimistic. (Sources: Reuters, AP, AFP, BBC, CNN, DW, Bloomberg, FT, WSJ, CNBC, Al Jazeera, TV5Monde.)

EUROPE'S ROLE IN THE TALKS. A sub-plot of the week was the fight over whether and how Europe participates. Putin initially said Europeans could join if they showed "readiness to contribute" (Reuters, Nov 13). Moscow then told Europe to pick a single envoy if it wants a seat at the table (FT). EU leaders squabbled over who to send (Bloomberg, DW, FT). Zelensky welcomed the prospect (Reuters, BBC). Europe fears a "Russian trap" (TV5Monde). Germany's Merz asked Trump for "no surprises" from the Putin talks (Reuters). This is still unresolved and will carry into next week.

THE TRUMP-XI-PUTIN TRILATERAL SUMMIT IN CHINA. Announced on November 13-14, this is the week's most consequential forward-looking event: Trump, Xi, and Putin will meet in Shenzhen on November 19, on the sidelines of APEC. It is the first three-way summit of the three great powers. The White House confirmed Trump will raise nuclear-arms cuts (Reuters, CNN, DW, Bloomberg, WSJ). The meeting evokes comparisons to Yalta in 1945 (AFP, Reuters). Beijing is described as facing a "Russia bind" (DW) and as wary of hosting (Reuters). The US balked at China's demand for a tightly scripted format (WSJ). This summit will dominate the second half of next week.

MILITARY ACTIONS ON RUSSIAN SOIL. The war is coming home to Russia in a very tangible way. Ukraine launched nearly 1,200 drones at Russia in a single day (AP, Nov 13). Ukraine hit its ninth Russian oil refinery since the start of November, including the biggest refinery in Siberia (Bloomberg). A drone attack sparked a fire at the Baltic port of Ust-Luga, injuring three (Reuters, Bloomberg). A Ukrainian drone struck a Russian warship in the Gulf of Finland, detected by Finland (Reuters, Bloomberg, Al Jazeera). Two car bombs hit Moscow in two days: one killed a Russian soldier near St Petersburg in a targeted assassination (Reuters, Nov 12), the other badly injured a former aide to a pro-Kremlin Ukrainian ex-PM (Reuters, BBC, CNN, DW, Al Jazeera). Ukraine claimed 3,000 Russian casualties in a single day (Al Jazeera). Russia's own records, per pirated official statistics, show over 400,000 Russian killed, and Al Jazeera reports the figure at 450,000. Over 11,000 foreign military deaths have been recorded by Russia (Bloomberg, TV5Monde). Russia also struck Ukrainian military factories, railways, food factories, and power infrastructure, with Kyiv facing winter blackouts (Reuters, DW, FT, BBC). (Sources: all outlets.)

RUSSIA'S ECONOMY, OIL, AND THE DIESEL DEAL. The Trump diesel deal, meant to bring Russian fuel back to US markets after sanctions were lifted, has stumbled. A tanker carrying Russian diesel made a U-turn off the US East Coast (WSJ, Bloomberg, Reuters). US companies are shunning the fuel (Reuters). Meanwhile, Russia's diesel exports to other markets doubled (FT), and oil revenues hit a five-month high (Bloomberg, CNBC). The IEA reported Russian fuel exports and oil output rebounded in October (Reuters). But the economy is slowing as Ukrainian strikes damage industry (Bloomberg). Russia is rationing petrol after refinery attacks (FT). Russia's push to replace the dollar with the Chinese yuan has collapsed (Bloomberg). Foreign businesses seized by Putin are helping fund the war machine (Bloomberg). (Sources: Bloomberg, FT, WSJ, CNBC, Reuters, Al Jazeera.)

SANCTIONS AND ECONOMIC PRESSURE. The EU agreed new sanctions listings on Russian banks, the shadow fleet, and misinformation operations (Reuters, Nov 11), with a formal package to be approved on Monday, November 17 (Reuters, Bloomberg). The UK sanctioned Russia's Slavneft oil producer (Reuters). Putin ordered a sanctioned Russian bank to seize a UK brokerage's assets (Bloomberg). The EU is also preparing Ukraine funding measures by year-end (Reuters). (Sources: Reuters, Bloomberg, FT.)

MEDIA, PRESS FREEDOM, AND INFORMATION WAR. Russia's last major independent newspaper, Novaya Gazeta, officially closed its Moscow newsroom after three decades, citing official pressure and eviction (Reuters, BBC, DW, CNN, TV5Monde). Two French deputies and two journalists from Le Monde and Ouest-France were barred from entering Russia (TV5Monde). Sberbank doubled down on AI after a drone attack on a data center (Reuters). Russia is using giant plastic bags to store unexported grain as Black Sea trade stalls (Reuters). (Sources: Reuters, BBC, DW, CNN, TV5Monde.)

ESPIONAGE AND INTELLIGENCE. A US Army soldier assigned to a NATO unit was arrested in the UK on suspicion of spying for Russia (AP, BBC, CNN, DW, Bloomberg, WSJ, Al Jazeera, TV5Monde). Russia arrested two suspected Polish spies in Kaliningrad (Reuters, Bloomberg). Romania's intelligence agency identified a Russian-linked cyber attack (Reuters). Norway's security service warned that Russian intelligence could carry out sabotage in the coming year (Reuters). The UK and Russia discussed the need for a new back channel to avoid miscalculation (FT). (Sources: all outlets.)

DOMESTIC POLITICS AND SOCIETY. A lawyer in Kaliningrad was sentenced to 12 years on treason charges (Reuters). Police raided Moscow gathering spots for young people (DW). Russia set cull limits to control the bear population after 36 bear attacks killed people (Reuters). Russia's ambassador to the US died suddenly at age 66 (Reuters, AP, CNN, Bloomberg). Russia's delegation visited Afghanistan to discuss trade with the Taliban (AP). Russia said military-to-military contacts with Britain are possible (Reuters). Russia said it could conclude non-aggression pacts with NATO members (Reuters). (Sources: Reuters, DW, AP, Bloomberg.)

SPORTS AND CULTURE. A wave of European countries barred Russian athletes: Norway (Reuters), Canada (Reuters, AP), Estonia (BBC), Finland (DW, Reuters). The IIHF filed a CAS challenge over Russia's reinstatement (Reuters). Russia threatened sanctions against Canada and Germany over the ice hockey dispute (DW). The NHL indicated Finland's block could affect future games (AP). (Sources: Reuters, AP, BBC, DW.)

OTHER NOTABLE ITEMS. Russia's top independent newspaper closing was a symbolic blow to dissent. Zelensky warned of Moscow seeking to redraw "influence" in Europe (AFP). Russia's shadow war has entered a "dangerous new phase" (Bloomberg). The US warned Madagascar over growing military ties with Russia (BBC). A "beer-loving nations alliance" (UK, Netherlands, Baltic states) was launched against Russian naval activity (TV5Monde). Russia and Ukraine are racing to build military satellite networks (Al Jazeera).

EU SANCTIONS PACKAGE (NOVEMBER 17). Almost certain: the EU will formally adopt the new sanctions package on Monday, November 17, targeting Russian banks, the shadow fleet, and misinformation operations, as agreed by EU envoys on November 11 and confirmed by France (Reuters, Bloomberg). The UK will likely add its own measures around the same time. Russia will issue a strong but not dramatic response. The sanctions will hit Sberbank, VTB, and several shadow fleet vessels. Expect some minor market jitters in the ruble. Confidence: almost certain the package is adopted; probable that Russia announces countermeasures within 48 hours.

PRISONER EXCHANGE EXECUTION. Probable: the "largest prisoner exchange" agreed in Abu Dhabi will be physically carried out in the days after November 14. Kushner explicitly said the US is working toward it (Reuters). The logistics of moving hundreds of prisoners across a front line take time, so I expect the actual swap to happen between November 15 and 21, possibly timed to coincide with or follow the Shenzhen summit for maximum photo opportunity. Confidence: probable it happens this week; possible it slips to early next week.

EUROPEAN DELEGATION FOR PEACE TALKS. Probable: the EU will finalize who its envoy or delegation to the next round of Russia-Ukraine talks will be. Moscow has set the condition: pick one person (FT). The EU's internal squabbling (Bloomberg, DW, FT) will resolve by mid-week. Expect a mix of foreign ministers or national security aides (Bloomberg mentioned national security aides). The next round of talks, if it happens, would likely be in late November or early December. Confidence: probable the EU agrees on a representative; possible a new round of talks is scheduled before the end of the month.

CONTINUED DRONE STRIKES ON RUSSIAN INFRASTRUCTURE. Almost certain: Ukraine will continue hitting Russian refineries, ports, and industrial zones. Nine refineries have been hit in November alone (Bloomberg). The Volgograd industrial zone was struck on November 13 (Reuters). The Samara oil-pumping station was hit on November 14 (Bloomberg). Expect at least two to four more significant strikes on Russian fuel and logistics infrastructure before November 21. Russia will respond with missile and drone strikes on Ukrainian power plants, railways, and food factories. The winter blackout risk in Ukraine will worsen as temperatures drop. Confidence: almost certain more strikes on both sides; probable that at least one major Russian refinery or port is hit again.

RUSSIAN DOMESTIC SECURITY AND CAR BOMBINGS. Possible: the two car bombings in Moscow within 48 hours (November 12 and 13) suggest a targeted campaign, possibly by Ukrainian intelligence or pro-Ukrainian factions. Expect heightened security in Moscow and St Petersburg. There may be one or two more targeted incidents, but a full wave of bombings is less likely in a single week. The Kaliningrad treason trial and the arrest of Polish spies suggest Russia is tightening its internal security net. Confidence: possible one more targeted incident; unlikely a major wave of domestic violence.

OIL AND DIESEL MARKET. Probable: the Russian diesel situation will remain messy. The US tanker U-turn (WSJ, Bloomberg) means the deal is not dead but not working. Russia will court Brazilian and other buyers (Reuters). Crude prices will be influenced by the Shenzhen summit outcome. If Trump and Putin signal a broader deal, oil may dip; if the summit is muted, prices hold. The IEA data showing a rebound in Russian exports (Reuters, CNBC) will be cited by both sides. Confidence: probable continued volatility; possible a small dip in crude prices after the summit.

SPORTS DISPUTES. Probable: the IIHF CAS challenge (Reuters) will be briefed or heard. Russia's threats of sanctions against Canada and Germany (DW) will generate more headlines. The World Juniors and figure skating worlds will remain in flux. No resolution expected this week. Confidence: probable the dispute continues; unlikely a final ruling before November 21.

NUCLEAR ARMS DISCUSSION. Probable: the Shenzhen summit will produce some language on a new or revised nuclear arms framework, but the actual negotiations will be technical and slow. Trump's goal is to get a headline; Putin's goal is to reset the strategic balance in Russia's favor. Xi will try to position China as a neutral broker. Expect a joint communique that sounds important but is vague on specifics. Confidence: probable a statement on nuclear arms; possible a framework for technical talks; unlikely a signed treaty.

LESS LIKELY SURPRISES (things that could happen but I would not bet heavily on):
- A sudden Russian offer to include the EU in the next round of talks, reversing Putin's earlier "pick one envoy" stance, if the Shenzhen summit goes well for him. (Possible, not probable.)
- A third car bombing or a more dramatic assassination in Moscow, escalating the domestic tension. (Possible.)
- A Russian cyberattack on European infrastructure in response to the new EU sanctions package, going beyond the Romanian incident. (Possible.)
- The US soldier espionage case in the UK being formally charged and generating a diplomatic spat. (Probable the charge is filed; the spasm is possible.)
- Russia announcing a new mobilization wave or a significant shift in front-line strategy, timed to the summit. (Unlikely to probable; Russia is more likely to use the summit as a stalling tool than to escalate.

THINGS I WOULD NOT BET ON:
- A full ceasefire or armistice signed this week. The talks are moving, but the gap between Russia's demands and Ukraine's positions is still wide. (Unlikely.)
- A major Russian offensive on the ground, like a new push toward a major city. Russia is in a defensive-stall posture while diplomacy is in play. (Unlikely.)
- The ruble crashing or a full-blown capital flight crisis triggered by the EU sanctions. The package is incremental, not transformative. (Unlikely.)
- Putin stepping down, being seen in a hospital, or any succession drama. He is meeting Trump and Xi in five days; he will not make a move now. (Very unlikely.)
- A Russian nuclear test or a dramatic escalation of the satellite race. The satellite networks are being built, but no launch event is expected. (Unlikely.)

That is a new, hard, dated event that did not exist in the first picture.

The yuan-replacement push collapsed, which is a new thread not present in the first picture.

crystal.forecast:
THE TRUMP-XI-PUTIN SUMMIT IN SHENZHEN (NOVEMBER 19). This is the dominant event of the week and will consume the second half. The summit is confirmed for November 19 in Shenzhen on the sidelines of APEC. Trump will raise nuclear-arms cuts, as the White House has confirmed. The format dispute between the US and China (Washington balked at Beijing's demand for a tightly scripted agenda) will either be resolved behind the scenes or will show in the body language of the photo op. The Yalta-1945 comparison will be in every headline. I expect a joint statement or a coordinated set of individual statements referencing nuclear arms, the Ukraine framework, and possibly a new European security architecture, but not a signed peace deal. Russia will enter with a hard line, as Putin was 'uncompromising' to Witkoff and Kushner in Moscow on November 12. The prisoner exchange from Abu Dhabi will be cited as proof of momentum. Zelensky will call it a 'window of opportunity' and push for European participation. The EU's unresolved question of who to send as a single envoy will create friction at the margins. China will position itself as a neutral broker while protecting its own trade interests. The summit will produce a photo, a statement, and a week of interpretation, but not a breakthrough. Confidence: very high that the summit happens as scheduled; high that it produces some form of joint or coordinated statement; medium that the nuclear-arms discussion produces a concrete next step; low that a full Ukraine framework is agreed.

EU SANCTIONS PACKAGE AND RUSSIAN COUNTERMEASURES (NOVEMBER 17). The EU's new sanctions listings on Russian banks, the shadow fleet, and misinformation operations are formally due for approval on Monday, November 17. This is a hard, dated event that will generate headlines across European and Russian media. The UK's sanctioning of Slavneft and Putin's order for a sanctioned bank to seize a UK brokerage's assets establish the pattern: Russia responds to each sanctions package with a targeted counter-move. I expect Russia to announce at least one concrete countermeasure within 48 hours of the EU vote: a new asset seizure, a targeted ban on a European company or bank, or a retaliatory trade restriction. The shadow-fleet listings will generate operational headaches for Russian oil exports, but the five-month-high oil revenues and the doubling of diesel exports to non-US markets suggest Russia has already begun redirecting. The sanctions will be framed in Moscow as 'coordinated European pressure' and in Brussels as 'a necessary step toward a credible framework.' Confidence: very high that the EU package is approved on or around November 17; high that Russia announces a countermeasure within a few days; medium that the countermeasure targets a specific, named European entity.

MILITARY ESCALATION ON RUSSIAN SOIL AND IN UKRAINE. The pattern of the past week is clear: 1,200 drones in a single day, the ninth refinery of November hit (including the biggest in Siberia), a warship struck in the Gulf of Finland, a fire at the port of Ust-Luga, and two car bombs in Moscow within two days. Ukraine is shifting toward urban, high-visibility targets inside Russia, not just industrial infrastructure. I expect at least two or three more significant strikes on Russian soil in the coming week, with a meaningful probability of another urban incident (a car bomb, a targeted assassination, or a drone strike on a building in a major city). Russia will continue striking Ukrainian energy, transport, and food infrastructure, worsening winter blackouts in Kyiv and other cities. The casualty numbers will continue to climb: the 400,000-plus Russian killed figure and the 11,000-plus foreign military deaths will be cited in new reports. The 46-square-miles-in-ten-months stat will remain background context, reinforcing the narrative of a grinding, costly war. Russia will not launch a major new ground offensive, but it will maintain pressure on the eastern and southern fronts. The satellite and military-communications race will continue as a background thread. Confidence: very high that significant strikes occur on both sides; high that at least one strike hits a Russian urban or port target; medium that a high-casualty event (20+ killed) occurs in a single incident; low that a new major ground offensive is launched.

FUEL, ENERGY, AND WINTER. Winter is arriving and the fuel crisis is deepening. Petrol rationing in several Russian regions will continue and may expand as refinery damage accumulates. The diesel deal with the US will see another stumble or a partial, grudging resolution: the tanker U-turn off the US East Coast and the shunning of Russian fuel by US companies suggest the deal is not yet working, but the political pressure from Trump (who will be in Shenzhen on November 19) may force a compromise. Russian oil revenues at a five-month high and the doubling of diesel exports to other markets give Moscow some breathing room, but the yuan-replacement collapse means Russia is still dependent on a fragmented, sanctions-affected trading system. Kyiv will face worsening winter blackouts as Russia strikes power infrastructure. Public complaints in Russian regions about fuel prices and availability will grow, though a mass street protest remains unlikely. The Sberbank AI and data-center story (after a drone hit) will generate further coverage as Russia pushes to modernize its military communications. Confidence: high that fuel rationing continues or expands; high that the diesel deal sees another complication; medium that a partial resolution is announced around the APEC summit; low that a mass fuel-price protest occurs in Moscow.

ESPIONAGE AND INTELLIGENCE. The cluster of espionage events this week (US Army soldier arrested in the UK for suspected Russian spying, two Polish spies arrested in Kaliningrad, a Russian-linked cyber attack identified in Romania, Norway's warning of possible sabotage, the UK-Russia back-channel discussion) is a new and persistent theme that the prior expectation model missed. I expect the US soldier case to generate diplomatic friction between London and Moscow, possibly a formal note or a low-level exchange. The UK-Russia back-channel will continue, and the Norway warning of possible sabotage in the coming year will be cited in European security briefings. There is a reasonable probability of one more arrest or revelation in Europe involving a Russian-linked operative or cyber incident. The Sberbank data-center drone hit and the broader military-satellite race will keep the intelligence-technology thread alive. Confidence: medium-high that the US soldier case generates a diplomatic response; medium that one more espionage-related arrest or revelation occurs in Europe; low that a major cyberattack on a single European financial institution occurs.

MEDIA, PRESS FREEDOM, AND INFORMATION WAR. Novaya Gazeta's closure of its Moscow newsroom will continue to generate commentary, both inside Russia and internationally. The barring of two French deputies and two journalists from entering Russia will be cited as evidence of a tightening information front. I expect at least one more media or information-war incident: a new cyberattack, a deepfake, a social-media manipulation story, or a further restriction on journalists. The state media will frame the Novaya Gazeta closure as 'a natural evolution' while independent and foreign media frame it as 'the last independent voice silenced.' The Russia-Ukraine information war will continue with both sides deploying battlefield narratives, possibly including new deepfake videos or hacked alert-app incidents. Confidence: high that Novaya Gazeta generates continued commentary; medium that one new information-war incident occurs; low that a major state-media reform or reversal is announced.

EUROPE'S ROLE AND THE ENVOY QUESTION. The EU's internal squabble over who to send as a single envoy to the Ukraine talks will remain unresolved, creating friction at the margins of the APEC summit. Zelensky will welcome European participation, and Putin will maintain that Europe can join if it shows 'readiness to contribute.' Germany's Merz will press Trump for 'no surprises' from the Putin talks. The EU's Ukraine funding measures due by year-end will be discussed but not finalized. The 'beer-loving nations alliance' (UK, Netherlands, Baltic states) against Russian naval activity will generate a small but persistent diplomatic thread. Confidence: medium that the envoy question is resolved before the end of the week; medium that the EU and Russia exchange pointed statements about European participation; low that a new European security framework is formally agreed.

ICE HOCKEY AND SPORTS. The dispute will continue as low-stakes, high-noise sparring. The IIHF's CAS challenge will be in the news, Russia will threaten or impose minor sanctions on Canada and Germany, and more European countries may join the boycott of Russian athletes. The NHL's position on Finland's block will be discussed. This is a sideshow, not a driver, but it generates consistent, low-intensity headlines. Confidence: high that the dispute continues without resolution; low that a compromise or CAS ruling changes the situation.

DOMESTIC POLITICS AND SOCIETY. The Kaliningrad lawyer's 12-year treason sentence and the police raids on Moscow youth gathering spots signal a tightening domestic grip. The sudden death of Russia's ambassador to the US at 66 will generate a brief news cycle and possibly a replacement announcement. The visit to Afghanistan to discuss trade with the Taliban will be a small but notable diplomatic thread. The bear-cull limits after 36 attacks are a small human-interest story. I do not expect a major domestic political event, but the social tension (youth raids, fuel rationing, casualty numbers) is building. Confidence: medium that the ambassador's death generates a replacement announcement; low that a significant domestic political crisis or protest occurs.

WHAT I WOULD NOT BET ON: A full peace deal signed in Shenzhen. A sudden Russian ceasefire timed to the summit. A major new Russian ground offensive. A mass Moscow street protest over fuel or the war. The Novaya Gazeta closure being reversed. A second major corporate seizure beyond the sanctions context. A nuclear test or exercise. A Black Sea attack on a non-belligerent vessel. Putin making a surprise personal concession on Donbas territory. The ice hockey dispute resolving before the end of the week.

crystal.eli5:
This week, three of the world's biggest leaders — the US president, the Chinese president, and the Russian president — are all flying to the same city in China to sit in a room together. It's the first time all three have met face-to-face, and everyone is watching to see if they can agree on anything, especially about nuclear weapons and the war in Ukraine. Think of it like three kids who've been arguing in the schoolyard finally being put in the same classroom by the principal. They'll probably shake hands and take a photo, but they won't necessarily agree on everything.

At the same time, the war is getting more intense and more personal for people living in Russia. Ukraine is sending huge waves of drones — over a thousand in a single day — and hitting oil refineries, a warship, and even dropping car bombs in Moscow. It's like the war, which used to feel like it was happening 'over there,' is now showing up in the streets of Russian cities. Meanwhile, Russia keeps hitting Ukraine's power plants and factories, making winter harder for people in Kyiv and other cities.

Europe is also stepping up. The EU is voting on a new set of rules that make it harder for Russia to do business and move its oil around the world. Russia will probably respond by grabbing some European company's assets, which is its usual move. And there's a whole undercurrent of spy stuff: a US soldier got arrested in the UK for allegedly spying for Russia, and there are arrests in Poland and Romania too. It's like the two sides are still playing a quiet game of cat-and-mouse even while they're trying to talk peace.

The fuel situation in Russia is getting worse as winter arrives. Gas stations are rationing, the deal to sell Russian diesel to the US keeps stumbling, and people in Russian regions are complaining about prices. But Russian oil revenues are actually at a five-month high because they're selling to other countries, so the picture is mixed: painful in some places, surprising in others.

The big question for the rest of the week is: does the Shenzhen meeting produce something real, or just a photo and a statement that both sides can spin as a win? Based on what's happened so far — the prisoner exchange, the 'uncompromising' Putin, the US pushing hard but not forcing a deal — the most likely outcome is a step forward, not a leap. The war doesn't end next week, but the diplomacy gets more personal and more public, and the strikes get more urban and more painful for ordinary Russians.

measurement.happened: This week in China was dominated by a single explosive story with dozens of ripple effects: the Nvidia spy scandal. Jensen Huang, CEO of the world's most valuable chip company, resigned after it emerged he had a long-running affair with Alice Huang, a Chinese businesswoman suspected of being a spy for Beijing. China's Ministry of State Security was thrust into the global spotlight (CNBC, Nov 12). China's foreign ministry and state media denied any spying, calling US claims 'baseless' and 'fabricated' (Al Jazeera Nov 12, Reuters Nov 9, BBC Nov 9). Yet the damage was done. A Chinese university was found to have bought Nvidia H200 chips despite the US blacklist (Reuters Nov 12, CNN Nov 12, Al Jazeera Nov 11). Alice Huang's linked firm procured banned Nvidia chips (Bloomberg Nov 13). Over three billion dollars in Chinese AI data-centre projects built on Nvidia hardware are now in doubt (Reuters Nov 13). Chinese AI firms scrambled to lock in Nvidia chip capacity before further US curbs (Reuters Nov 13). The US Justice Department has not formally concluded Huang was a Chinese spy, but the FBI is investigating (Reuters Nov 12, BBC Nov 10, CNN Nov 12). Huang was summoned to testify before Congress (BBC Nov 13). Treasury Secretary Bessent publicly blamed Commerce Secretary Lutnick's department for letting chips 'leak' to China (CNBC Nov 13). A shareholder lawsuit was filed against Nvidia (DW Nov 10). Trump had been briefed about the relationship during his May trip to China (WSJ Nov 10, CNBC Nov 10). The Wall Street Journal ran an exclusive on a 'vast Chinese spying machine' behind the affair (WSJ Nov 14). Former CIA officers called it a classic Chinese honeypot pattern (CNBC Nov 9). China's AI stocks sold off sharply (FT Nov 13, Bloomberg Nov 13), though BofA called the selloff overdone (CNBC Nov 12). China warned the US not to use the scandal as a pretext for a broader tech blockade (FT Nov 12, Al Jazeera Nov 12). The scandal also revealed Singapore's role as a transit hub in China's AI chip trade (FT Nov 11, CNBC Nov 13). In short, the affair became a proxy war over who controls the AI chip supply chain, and Beijing was the biggest loser, according to Bloomberg (Nov 12). The second major theme was the announcement of a historic trilateral summit. On November 14, the White House confirmed that Trump, Xi, and Putin would meet in China on November 19 for the first-ever three-way gathering, focused on nuclear non-proliferation (BBC Nov 14, Bloomberg Nov 14, CNN Nov 13, Al Jazeera Nov 14, WSJ Nov 14, AFP Nov 14). The US had initially balked at China's demand for a tightly scripted format (WSJ Nov 9). Officials said Trump would not raise the Nvidia spy issue at the summit (FT Nov 14, CNBC Nov 14). The meeting is being framed as a nuclear arms discussion, but it is clearly also about positioning the US, China, and Russia for the next phase of great-power competition (DW Nov 14, Bloomberg Nov 12). The third theme was trade. China's goods trade surplus surpassed one trillion dollars for the second consecutive year, with exports surging 35 percent in the first ten months (AP Nov 10, WSJ Nov 10, FT Nov 10, TV5Monde Nov 10). The US and China held their first-ever Board of Trade meeting, discussing tariffs and farm trade (Reuters Nov 13, Bloomberg Nov 14). Bessent called for more balanced trade ties (AP Nov 11, CNBC Nov 11). China's Singles' Day shopping festival struggled to shake off weak consumer spending (AP Nov 11), while passenger car exports surged as domestic demand stayed soft (AP Nov 12). The central bank vowed to step up policy support (Reuters Nov 11, WSJ Nov 12). Credit growth disappointed despite greater policy support (Bloomberg Nov 13). Producer inflation accelerated to a four-year high (WSJ Nov 14). The market regulator warned of global asset repricing risks (Bloomberg Nov 14). China's trade surplus is a source of both pride and anxiety, as Al Jazeera noted it is not all good news (Nov 11). The fourth theme was Taiwan. Xi renewed his call for 'complete reunification,' saying history cannot be stopped (Reuters Nov 12, DW Nov 12, Al Jazeera Nov 12, Al Jazeera Nov 12). China staged unannounced Pacific military drills described as 'silent intimidation' of Taiwan (Reuters Nov 13). The G7 foreign ministers said China's actions east of Taiwan threaten stability (Reuters Nov 12). Taiwan's president said the island is taking part in the APEC summit in China on an 'equal basis' (Reuters Nov 12). Taiwan appointed Acer's founder as its APEC envoy and called for written guarantees from China (Reuters Nov 11). Violent attacks on critics of China in Taiwan raised concerns about transnational repression (AP Nov 14). The fifth theme was domestic political drama and governance. A COVID-era Wuhan party boss was placed under investigation by the anti-graft watchdog (Reuters Nov 13). A dissident artist was jailed for satirical Mao sculptures (DW Nov 13). A man smashed a Chinese government building with an excavator, captured on video (BBC Nov 10). Bloomberg ran a piece on Xi Jinping's succession dilemma (Nov 12). The sixth theme was China's growing global footprint in energy, shipping, and industry. China signed a preliminary deal to invest fifteen billion dollars in solar and wind in Turkey (Reuters Nov 12). CNOOC reported a major ultra-deep gas discovery in the Bohai Sea (Reuters Nov 12). China decided to meet all new power demand with clean energy (Bloomberg Nov 14). China is building a rival to the centuries-old Lloyd's of London for shipping insurance (WSJ Nov 13, Nov 12). China is taking aim at Western dominance of the gas-turbine industry (Bloomberg Nov 12). Bangladesh picked a Chinese firm to build a third floating LNG terminal (Reuters Nov 12). China's chemical supply chain is fueling the US opioid crisis (Bloomberg Nov 13). The seventh theme was science, space, and health. Pakistan's first astronaut will fly with China (DW Nov 13, DW Nov 10). China fired researchers after a child died in a gene-editing trial (Bloomberg Nov 13). Eli Lilly became the first drugmaker to have a GLP-1 weight-loss pill approved in China (Reuters Nov 12). China's Moonshot AI restructured to pave the way for an IPO (WSJ Nov 14). SMIC doubled its profit on an AI boost (WSJ Nov 12). SigmaStar plans a three-hundred-million-dollar HK listing (Bloomberg Nov 13). The eighth theme was broader diplomatic activity. South Korea's foreign minister met China's Wang, with the Korean side saying it should not fear China's rise (Reuters Nov 14, Nov 13). China and ASEAN made progress on a South China Sea pact but could not finish talks this year (AP Nov 11). China and India achieved a diplomatic thaw but the border is flaring up again (DW Nov 11). Japan's PM Takaichi will attend the APEC summit in China amid degraded relations (TV5Monde Nov 13). The US and China agreed on the importance of leader-level talks to advance denuclearization (Reuters Nov 11). China's access to some Nvidia chips is in doubt as curbs gain traction in Congress (Reuters Nov 12). In sum, this was a week in which a personal scandal at a US tech company became a geopolitical earthquake, a historic three-power summit was locked in for November 19, trade tensions simmered beneath a record surplus, and Taiwan remained the flashpoint closest to a breaking point.

And then there's Taiwan, which is always on the radar, with China doing military drills and saying they want the island back 'eventually.' None of these things are new, but they all get louder when three world leaders are in the same room.

measurement.happened:
This week in DR Congo was dominated by three major threads: a worsening Ebola crisis, a bold constitutional power grab by President Tshisekedi, and continued bloodshed in the east.

Ebola remains the story of the week and arguably the biggest. Cases passed 11,000 with 5,387 deaths, making it the deadliest outbreak the country has seen, according to Al Jazeera and Reuters. MSF declared the outbreak still out of control after six months, and warned that millions of dollars in funding are going missing while the virus keeps spreading (BBC, Bloomberg, TV5Monde). The CDC and Africa CDC both flagged that attacks on health workers are actively hampering the response (Reuters, TV5Monde). Merck urged wider deployment of the Ervebo vaccine against the Bundibugyo strain (Bloomberg, TV5Monde). The outbreak is also hitting the economy: Barrick Gold furloughed some employees at its Congo mine as an Ebola precaution (Reuters), and a metals trader backed by quants is in talks to secure a tin deal, suggesting commodity markets are watching the outbreak closely (Bloomberg). On top of Ebola, Deutsche Welle reported the return of cholera, raising fears of a compounded health emergency. TV5Monde noted hundreds of millions of dollars have been poured into the response with visible gaps remaining.

On the political front, President Félix Tshisekedi signed a contested referendum law that opens the door to a new Constitution and, by extension, a third term in office (Reuters, TV5Monde, Bloomberg, BBC). Parliament had passed the law, and the move is seen as a constitutional gamble, as Bloomberg put it. The timing is notable because it lands while the country is in the middle of a major health crisis and ongoing wars in the east. In a related power play, the government announced it wants to rename streets and public places that bear the name of former president Joseph Kabila (TV5Monde), a symbolic erasure that is already sparking debate. Meanwhile, Lambert Mende, a former close ally of Kabila, publicly threw his support behind Tshisekedi (TV5Monde), signaling a shift in the political alliances around the president. The government also pushed to make Étienne Tshisekedi, Félix's late father, one of five national heroes, a move that is generating controversy (TV5Monde).

The military and conflict situation in the east remains grim. At least 66 Congolese soldiers were sentenced to death for what the authorities called cowardice and revolt before the enemy in the fight against FRN rebels (BBC, Deutsche Welle, TV5Monde). Islamic State-affiliated ADF rebels killed at least 22 to 66 civilians in a single week in the east, including three health workers (AP, TV5Monde). BBC also carried a headline referencing M23 activity, suggesting the rebel landscape is multi-front. The death sentences for soldiers are a dramatic escalation in military discipline that will likely ripple through the armed forces.

At the Francophonie summit, DR Congo and Rwanda clashed over the leadership of the OIF. DRC proposed withdrawing its candidate and called on Rwanda to do the same, and signaled it was ready to back a Romanian candidate to block the Rwandan bid (TV5Monde, multiple dates). This is a proxy for the deeper RDC-Rwanda rivalry playing out in a multilateral setting. The summit became a stage for the two neighbors to jockey for influence among Francophone African states.

In lighter news, DR Congo played Africa Cup of Nations qualifiers against Comoros and Sierra Leone, with Watford midfielder Edo Kayembe scoring for the national team (BBC). A Reuters feature highlighted Congolese coders using AI to rescue school records lost to war, a small but human story. TV5Monde also ran a piece on DRC's ambition to transform its minerals domestically rather than exporting raw ore, signaling an industrial policy push.

On top of Ebola, cholera is also spreading, so hospitals are dealing with two diseases at the same time with the same tired staff.

The war is not just against one group; there are at least two or three different rebel forces fighting in different areas, and there is no sign of a peace deal coming soon.
