judged.reading_a: Forecast A correctly identified Ebola as the dominant story and nailed the death toll at 5,500, which matched the UN figure reported by Reuters. It also correctly predicted the Barrick Gold furlough, the Africa CDC/WHO warnings about the outbreak being out of control, and the DRC-Rwanda diplomatic sparring around the Francophonie summit. Its prediction that the Francophonie clash would produce statements and diplomatic notes was broadly right, as the DRC threatened to quit and Macron urged unity. However, A significantly overestimated the Ebola case count, predicting 12,000 to 13,000 when the actual figure was just past 6,000. A also overemphasized several threads that were not prominent this week: the parallel cholera epidemic (not a major headline), the killing of health workers by ADF specifically (M23 dominated rebel coverage), the 66 death sentences rippling through the army (not a major story), and the constitutional/symbolic campaign (street renamings, Tshisekedi as national hero, C64 opposition rally, Lambert Mende realignment). A's prediction of a Merck/Ervebo procurement update was close in spirit to the WHO's announcement of strain-specific vaccine trials, but the specific framing was off. A missed the US-DRC bilateral mineral agreement as a major political story, the US Democrats' push to investigate Trump's African mineral deals, the 'resources curse' framing, the OIF two-month timeline, and the retraining of former Congo fighters in Rwanda. A's overall picture was directionally correct on the big themes but over-specified on several sub-threads that did not materialize, and it got the scale of the Ebola caseload wrong by roughly a factor of two.
judged.reading_b: Forecast B also correctly identified Ebola as the dominant story and the DRC-Rwanda/M23 tension as a major thread. It correctly predicted that the outbreak would remain out of control, that case numbers would climb, and that the death toll would tick upward. Its prediction of diplomatic sparring from Kinshasa or Kigali was confirmed by the DRC threatening to quit the Francophonie. B correctly noted that M23 could resurface, which it did as a major thread. It also correctly identified the Barrick furlough and the OIF leadership question. However, B also overestimated the Ebola case count, predicting above 11,000 when the actual was around 6,000, though its error was less dramatic than A's. B did not over-predict the cholera epidemic, the ADF-specific violence, or the constitutional/symbolic campaign, all of which were not major stories this week. B missed the US-DRC mineral deal as a major political story (it mentioned 'tin-deal talks' in passing but not the broader bilateral agreement or the US political dimension), the WHO strain-specific vaccine trial announcement, the 'resources curse' framing, and the US Democrats' investigation push. B's list of 'less likely surprises' (power outage, cabinet reshuffle, cholera cluster, coup) all did not happen, which is fine since they were labeled unlikely. B's overall picture was more conservative and fewer of its specific predictions were contradicted by the actual week.
judged.comparison: Both forecasts got the two dominant themes right: Ebola as the overwhelming story and the DRC-Rwanda/M23/Francophonie diplomatic clash. Both correctly identified the Barrick furlough and the general trajectory of the outbreak. Both missed the US-DRC bilateral mineral agreement as a major political story and the WHO vaccine trial announcement, which were significant concrete developments. The key differences are in the sub-threads. Forecast A made more specific predictions that did not materialize: the parallel cholera epidemic as a major headline, ADF-specific violence (when M23 dominated), the 66 death sentences generating visible army reactions, street renamings, the C64 opposition rally, and the Tshisekedi national-hero debate. A also overestimated the Ebola case count by roughly a factor of two (12,000-13,000 vs. 6,000). Forecast B was more restrained, hedged more, and made fewer specific predictions that could be contradicted. B correctly foregrounded M23 alongside ADF, did not invent a cholera parallel, and kept the constitutional thread as context rather than a major predicted event. B's Ebola number (above 11,000) was still off but less dramatically so. B's list of unlikely surprises all stayed unlikely, which is a small point in its favor. A's death toll prediction of 5,500 was spot on, which is a point for A. But A's extra specificity cost it more in misses than it gained in hits. For a reader trying to understand what the coming week would look like, B's more measured and fewer-numbered predictions gave a cleaner and more accurate picture, while A's detailed but over-confident sub-predictions (cholera, ADF, street renamings, C64 rally, Merck/Ervebo) added noise and some misdirection. Neither forecast captured the US mineral deal as a major political story, which was a notable shared blind spot. measurement.happened:
The dominant story of the week was the strange, uneasy status of the US-Iran war: simultaneously declared 'effectively over' by President Trump and yet still producing fresh strikes, mine-laying, and threats. On November 9, after meeting the Qatari prime minister in Washington, Trump told reporters the war was militarily 'effectively over' and that further airstrikes were 'highly unlikely.' He repeated this message on Veterans Day, saying 'we won,' and again on November 14, telling advisers he may hold off on attacks barring new provocations. Yet the same week brought a US strike on Iran's Kharg Island, an Iranian drone or missile shot at an early-warning radar site in Bahrain (which the US denied), Iran's attack on shipping navigation systems on Oman's Didamar island, and a naval blockade ordered to begin the following night. The picture is one of a war that has no formal end but also no clear active phase: a grinding, low-intensity confrontation with periodic spikes of violence. Headlines from Reuters, AP, BBC, Bloomberg, WSJ, CNBC, and Al Jazeera all confirm this limbo.

The Strait of Hormuz was the most active and consequential theater. Between November 12 and 14, the IRGC and Iranian navy reported that at least four to five tankers and an LNG carrier were hit by sea mines or explosions while transiting the strait. One tanker caught fire. Iran's chief negotiator Ghalibaf declared that Hormuz will 'never return' to its pre-war status and that the strait will stay restricted until Iranian demands are met. The UN urged both sides to allow fertilizer shipments through immediately. Meanwhile the US moved aircraft out of two UK bases over Iran threats, and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent was relocated to a military base after what sources described as 'growing Iranian threats.' Bessent later told reporters, 'F the Iranian leadership.' The maritime crisis is clearly the main lever both sides are using: Iran to squeeze global energy and trade, the US to pressure Iran's oil revenue. Headlines from Reuters, Al Jazeera, DW, Bloomberg, and WSJ all document this.

The nuclear file moved in a negative direction. The IAEA issued a report expressing 'increasing concern' over an uninspected Iranian enrichment plant. Iran told the agency that monitoring cannot proceed while it is under military threat. Iran's security chief declared the country will not allow enriched nuclear material to leave the country. Iran also asked the UN to condemn a $20 million US bounty for nuclear intelligence. Bloomberg reported that Iran extended its blackout of nuclear work with the US. At the same time, Iran backed a nuclear treaty in principle even as hardliners raised the prospect of a bomb. Canada reimposed sanctions on eleven Iranian entities tied to nuclear activities. The net effect is that the nuclear dimension is frozen in a tense, adversarial posture with no inspection access and no visible progress. Headlines from Reuters, BBC, AP, Bloomberg, and Al Jazeera support this.

A genuinely new and unusual story broke: France accused Iran's Revolutionary Guards (specifically the Shahid Kaveh cyberunit) of carrying out what it called an 'unprecedented' cyberattack that caused supermarket refrigerators across France to heat up, potentially spoiling food. France summoned Iran's ambassador and warned it 'does not rule out anything' in its response. Belgium's ministers were at odds over Iran's role. Iran denied responsibility. The US also suspected Iran's involvement. This was the first time Iran had been publicly blamed for a cyberattack with real-world physical consequences in Europe, and the Wall Street Journal framed it as part of a new Iranian cyber playbook aimed at creating tangible havoc. Headlines from Reuters, AP, AFP, CNN, DW, TV5Monde, Bloomberg, WSJ, FT, and CNBC all cover this.

US domestic politics collided with the Iran war. Democrats won the midterms, and a Reuters/Ipsos poll found most Americans want the new Congress to end the war. Trump himself acknowledged the war 'played a role' in the Republican loss. He then sidelined Vice President JD Vance, telling him to shift focus from Iran to 'corruption and crime' at home, and declared 'we don't need a deal with Iran.' This was a significant reversal, as Vance had been emerging as the lead negotiator and was heading to Pakistan for talks. Defense Secretary Hegseth faced an impeachment push from Rep. Thomas Massie over the war. Shutdown risks emerged as Democrats considered legislative ways to end the conflict. The split within the Trump team between Rubio (blockade and pressure) and Vance (diplomatic deal) became public. Headlines from Reuters, AP, CNN, Bloomberg, WSJ, FT, CNBC, DW, and Al Jazeera document this political turbulence.

Iran's military and intelligence activities continued at a low but persistent level. Iran lifted its 2,000-kilometer range limit on ballistic missiles. Bloomberg reported Iran is producing roughly 50 missiles per month despite a crippled defense industry. Iran opened a new training camp for women in readiness for war. Iran designated Argentina's navy and air force as 'terrorist organizations' in a reciprocal move. In the UK, two Iranian men were convicted of spying on journalists and a lawyer. The US Justice Department charged three alleged Iranian operatives over a plot to attack RAF Fairford, with one operative directing the plan via coded messages from a New York jail. The US moved military aircraft from two UK bases. These episodes show Iran's intelligence and covert action network is active in Europe and the Gulf. Headlines from Reuters, AP, CNN, DW, Bloomberg, WSJ, and Al Jazeera confirm this.

The economic fallout continued to ripple. Oil prices fell to a ten-week low on de-escalation hopes, then rebounded when Trump said no deal was needed. OPEC+ output in October neared pre-war levels, led by Saudi Arabia. India's Gulf oil imports surpassed Russian imports for the first time. European gas prices rose on winter uncertainty. Iran warned of domestic gas shortages this winter. Canada hiked interest rates to contain the oil-price shock. The US Treasury warned against rate hikes during the energy shock. US oil giants reported profit surges. The overall picture is a global economy still adjusting to a prolonged, unresolved energy disruption. Headlines from Reuters, Bloomberg, DW, CNBC, FT, and Al Jazeera support this.

Diplomacy was active but stalled. Vance was heading to Pakistan for talks. Egypt's top diplomat expressed hope for a US-Iran agreement 'in coming days.' Iran's chief negotiator told Al Jazeera the 'ball is in the US court.' The G7 foreign ministers met in Paris to discuss Iran. The Qatari prime minister visited Washington. Iran told COP31 it wants compensation for environmental damage from US-Israeli strikes. Yet Iran's top security official said no talks were underway with the US, and Iran defended a two-day proposal for peace talks that the US had rejected. The result was a week of parallel diplomatic tracks, none of them producing a breakthrough. Headlines from Reuters, AP, DW, Bloomberg, WSJ, FT, CNBC, and Al Jazeera cover this.

Finally, there were smaller but notable stories: Iran's president attended COP31. A Nobel Peace Prize winner, Narges Mohammadi, released a memoir. Iranian women were photographed daring greater freedom in dress despite restrictions. Exiled journalists reported continued repression. Iraq barred the plane carrying Iran's soccer team from landing in Basra over US sanctions. A new satellite image revealed the extent of Iran's missile bases. The UN reported 25 seafarers killed in or around Hormuz since the war began. These human and cultural threads remind us that the war is reshaping daily life inside Iran and its diaspora.

crystal.eli5:
Imagine two kids in a playground who both say the fight is over, but one keeps throwing pebbles and the other keeps pushing the other's stuff off the bench. That is what is happening between the United States and Iran right now. President Trump says the war is done and America won, but ships are still getting hit in the Strait of Hormuz, the US Navy is still blockading Iranian ports, and both sides are still making threats. For the next week, expect more ships to be hit in that narrow waterway between Iran and the Gulf. Iran has said the strait will never go back to normal, and the US has said it will keep its naval blockade in place. So both sides are squeezing each other through the sea.

Back in Washington, the new Congress, which is now controlled by Democrats, is going to press hard on the war. They want to know why the US is still spending money and risking sailors if the war is over. There is a push to impeach the Defense Secretary, and there is a risk that the government could shut down if the two sides in Congress cannot agree on a budget. Trump is trying to manage all of this by saying he does not need a deal with Iran and that America already won. But that makes it harder for him to explain why the Navy is still out there.

There is also a weird new story about France, where Iran was accused of hacking supermarket refrigerators so the food inside would heat up and go bad. It sounds almost like a joke, but it is serious: it is the first time Iran has been publicly blamed for a cyberattack that caused physical damage in Europe. France is getting angry and may impose sanctions or do a cyberattack of its own. Iran is denying it, but the US and Belgium are also looking into it. Meanwhile, Iranian spies are still active in the UK and France, and there are more arrests and charges expected. The nuclear question is stuck: Iran will not let inspectors in, the US will not stop sanctioning, and nobody is moving toward a deal. The whole thing is a slow, grinding pressure that neither side can easily end, and both sides are testing how far they can push before the other one snaps.

A misread the baseline: the 'status quo' was a lull, not a grinding stalemate, and it broke. That said, A's 25-to-30 percent probability for 'a significant new US air or missile campaign' landed close to what happened (the Qeshm strike and hits on Iranian infrastructure). A correctly called the absence of a formal ceasefire or deal, the Hormuz tanker and mine incidents (though it expected one or two, and there were more), the nuclear freeze, the continuation of multi-track diplomacy (Qatar, Pakistan, Egypt), and the rise of US domestic politics around the war (Senate blocking a resolution, shutdown struggle, Trump's Veterans Day defense). A's cyber section focused heavily on the France-fridge-hack follow-through, which was less prominent than expected; the actual espionage stories (North Macedonia/Greece assassination plot, UK RAF Fairford trial, Pakistani man's 27-year sentence) were broader and more varied. measurement.happened:
This week in Israel was dominated by the swearing-in of a new Knesset and the immediate scramble to form a government, set against a backdrop of continued and intensifying strikes on Gaza, a worsening humanitarian crisis as winter floods hit, and a visible shift in US political support. Here is what happened, theme by theme.

NEW KNESSET AND GOVERNMENT FORMATION. The single biggest political event was the swearing-in of the new Israeli parliament on November 10, after a highly contested election in which neither Benjamin Netanyahu nor his main rival Gadi Eisenkot secured a clear majority (Reuters, BBC, DW, TV5Monde, Bloomberg, Al Jazeera). Eisenkot was given the mandate to form a government and immediately unveiled an agenda to reverse Netanyahu's key policies, including a proposed independent probe into the events of October 7, 2024 (DW, Bloomberg, Al Jazeera). He called on the Arab parties to join a coalition, acknowledging he needs their votes (Bloomberg, TV5Monde). Netanyahu, now in an interim or opposition role, called for a unity government and accused Eisenkot of using 'tricks' to block the process, while Eisenkot in turn slammed Netanyahu's 'racist' campaign against Palestinian Israelis (AFP, TV5Monde, Al Jazeera). The Israeli president publicly warned against a repeat election, signalling pressure on both camps to compromise (Al Jazeera, TV5Monde). The BBC ran a Somali-language headline framing the contest as a fight over who can build a new government, and Al Jazeera published a detailed piece on what powers Netanyahu retains as interim PM. Bloomberg noted that Netanyahu's opponents in Parliament moved to undo his key policies within days, and that Eisenkot faces tough odds in building a coalition. CNN framed the week as Netanyahu's grip on power weakening. Al Jazeera's editorial argued that even if Netanyahu falls, his far-right legacy in Israeli politics is 'going nowhere,' and a separate piece examined how personality politics under Netanyahu has reshaped Israeli democracy.

GAZA STRIKES AND THE HOSPITAL BOMBING. The most lethal and symbolically damaging event was the Israeli strike on Gaza's Nasser Hospital on November 12, which killed at least six people including a surgeon, a child, and other medics, and hit the intensive-care unit (Reuters, AP, BBC, CNN, DW, FT, WSJ, Al Jazeera, TV5Monde). Israel said a senior Hamas figure was inside the hospital (DW, Al Jazeera). TV5Monde reported it as the deadliest single day in Gaza since the Israeli elections, with 11 killed across multiple strikes that day. Other strikes throughout the week killed dozens more: a father and son, two brothers, a six-year-old burn victim caught in an aid dispute, a Palestinian footballer Mahmoud Kamal Abdel-Malek, and a goalkeeper days after playing in a cup honouring slain athletes (Reuters, AP, Al Jazeera). The FT noted the strike came despite a ceasefire, and Al Jazeera ran a series of pieces on how Israel is 'expanding its war on healthcare.' The BBC and AP both highlighted the strike as emblematic of the devastation to Gaza's healthcare system.

GAZA HUMANITARIAN CRISIS AND WINTER FLOODS. Winter arrived hard on Gaza. Rain and flooding compounded the damage from the war: a sand embankment collapsed onto tents killing four (Reuters, TV5Monde), a baby died from cold amid Israeli restrictions on aid (Al Jazeera), families described hands 'as cold as ice' (Al Jazeera), and WHO warned respiratory illnesses would rise as winter floods arrived (Reuters). UNICEF said Israel was blocking repairs to Gaza's drainage basins, warning of flood risk (Reuters). The Board of Peace, a Trump-era body, called the situation an 'immediate humanitarian emergency' and said Israel's aid response was 'insufficient' (FT, BBC, Bloomberg, Al Jazeera). Al Jazeera published a long piece on how Gaza's infrastructure collapse leaves residents defenceless against floods, and another on how with every rainfall Gaza risks losing access to power and healthcare. F1 champion Lewis Hamilton visited the Rafah crossing to see aid efforts and urged Israel to let more aid in (Reuters, Al Jazeera). The EU called for immediate humanitarian access to Gaza (Al Jazeera). TV5Monde ran a video on the urgency after the floods and a chronicle titled 'In Gaza' about a war that hits journalists in their own homes.

US POLITICS AND THE MIDTERMS. The US midterm elections produced a noticeable shift. Trump said a 'great dislike' for Israel contributed to Republican losses (CNN). Bloomberg ran a piece arguing the GOP's shift away from Israel was 'inevitable,' while Nikki Haley called it 'completely misguided' to blame Israel for midterm losses (Bloomberg). The FT published a major piece titled 'How Israel lost America,' and Al Jazeera asked whether Washington is rethinking its relationship with Israel and whether Democrats will try to strip the US-Israel initiative from Pentagon funding. The AP noted that the US midterms put the pro-Israel powerhouse AIPAC on the defensive. Bloomberg asked what Israel stands to lose as US support fades. The US Ambassador to Israel, Mike Huckabee, was seen visiting the West Bank on November 14 (DW).

IRAN AND REGIONAL TENSIONS. Iran told the COP31 climate summit it wants compensation for environmental damage from US-Israeli strikes (Reuters). Netanyahu and Eisenkot clashed publicly over whether Israel should strike Iran again (Bloomberg). Al Jazeera ran a piece on whether Netanyahu can launch a strike on Iran before he leaves office, and another on 'Iranophobia' as Netanyahu's bid to transform fear into political survival. Iran warned of expanded retaliation as Israel reportedly readies to attack (Al Jazeera). The Houthis said they carried out a second attack targeting Israel (DW). Al Jazeera reported that 25 seafarers have been killed in or around the Strait of Hormuz since the US-Israel war on Iran, and that Trump said Israel and Gulf allies must repay the cost of the Iran war.

LEBANON. The US announced it would mediate new Lebanon-Israel peace talks, with a new round of negotiations set to take place in the US (DW). Al Jazeera noted Israel is 'disrupting entire ecosystems' in Lebanon, including its wheat crop.

FRANCE AND THE MELENCHON BAN. Israel banned French hard-left leader Jean-Luc Melenchon from entering its territory, and France publicly criticised the move as 'demagogic' (Reuters, TV5Monde, Al Jazeera, AP). A separate incident saw a prominent Israeli settler denied entry into France (Al Jazeera). These two reciprocal acts of diplomatic friction underscored the growing transatlantic and European tensions.

WEST BANK AND SYRIA. Israeli forces killed a Palestinian boy in the West Bank (BBC). Al Jazeera published an investigation arguing that Israeli soldiers in the West Bank are 'also settlers.' Israeli settlers burned down a business near Nablus in a massive fire (Al Jazeera). In Syria, Israel detained dozens of Syrians, and families are desperate for answers; photos showed daily life in Syrian villages disrupted by Israeli raids (AP).

ECONOMY AND BUSINESS. Murphy Oil announced entry into the Eastern Mediterranean with Zone G license awards offshore Israel (FT). A humanoid robot start-up backed by Eric Trump is in talks with Israel's military (FT). Vine Ventures launched a fund focused on US-Israeli tech ties (WSJ). India bypassed its own rules to buy Israeli phone-hacking technology (Al Jazeera). The BDS movement claimed a win as energy giants quit an Israeli gas project off Gaza (Al Jazeera). The UK aimed sanctions at Israel that also hit the Cayman Islands (WSJ). ImmunityBio and Rafa announced Israeli Ministry of Health approval of a bladder cancer treatment (FT).

SPORTS AND CULTURE. Kosovo fans booed and whistled the Israeli national anthem before a 0-0 Nations League draw (AP). Republic of Ireland players spoke about the stress of handling Israel games in the UEFA Nations League (BBC, AP). The Israeli bobsleigh team was at the centre of a Swiss TV commentary dispute (AFP). Under the baton of Daniel Barenboim, Israelis and Palestinians performed together for peace (TV5Monde). Israel killed a Gaza goalkeeper days after he played in a cup honouring slain athletes (Al Jazeera).

NATURAL EVENTS AND MISC. An earthquake in the Eilat region briefly closed Ramon Airport before flights resumed (Reuters). A video from Berlin was misrepresented online as showing a Palestinian flag over the Knesset (AFP). A rights group raised concerns about a jailed doctor, Dr Abu Safia, amid the strikes (Al Jazeera). A Thai PM told the Israeli envoy that foreigners are treated equally, likely in response to a diplomatic incident (Bloomberg).

crystal.eli5:
Imagine a class where the teacher just changed, and the old teacher is still in the room making loud comments. That's Israel right now. A new parliament was sworn in, and a man named Eisenkot is trying to build a team of ministers to run the country. But the old leader, Netanyahu, is still around, making public speeches, accusing Eisenkot of cheating, and trying to get his own people back into the picture. Nobody has agreed on a team yet, and they're arguing loudly in public. This will probably continue all week, and by the end of the week, there may still not be a confirmed government. That means decisions are being made by people who aren't fully in charge yet, which makes things messier.

In Gaza, a hospital was bombed and a surgeon and a child died. That's a big deal because hospitals are supposed to be safe places. On top of that, winter rain is falling, tents are flooding, babies are getting cold, and the world's health organizations are saying it's an emergency. The strikes are continuing, and the weather is making everything worse. Think of it like a house with a leaky roof and someone keeps throwing rocks through the windows. The rocks are the bombs, and the rain is the winter. Both are happening at the same time, and the people inside are getting more and more hurt.

In the United States, the elections just changed the political mood. The new leaders in Congress are less automatically in favor of Israel, and the president has said he has a 'great dislike' for the country. That doesn't mean the relationship is over, but it means Israel can no longer assume the US will always have its back. This is making Israeli leaders anxious and pushing them to act quickly on things like the war in Gaza and the relationship with Iran, because the window of unqualified US support is visibly getting smaller. Meanwhile, in the sea between Yemen and Saudi Arabia, the Houthi rebels have attacked twice, and 25 sailors have been killed. That's a lot of people, and it makes everyone in the region nervous about a third attack.

judged.reading_a: Forecast A saw much of the week's direction correctly. Its 'almost certain' calls on continued Gaza strikes, winter worsening, and the post-midterm US political shift all materialized. The prediction that Netanyahu would press for a unity government and that a public clash with Eisenkot would dominate was spot-on: Netanyahu called for unity on November 14 and Eisenkot dismissed it as 'tricks.' The Board of Peace pressure, the humanitarian winter crisis, and the US congressional friction all arrived as forecast. The 'unlikely' calls (no full government, no snap election, no full-scale ground offensive) were largely correct, though the ground operation on November 18 was a limited breach of that 'unlikely' bucket. The Melenchon-ban-triggered sanctions surprise was partially right in spirit (European sanctions did land) but wrong in specifics (UK and Australia, not France/EU; triggered by settlements, not the Melenchon ban). What A missed or underweighted: the Knesset speaker election as the week's defining political moment. A framed the political story around coalition-building talks and public spats, which were present, but the actual headline event was the election of Matan Kahana as speaker, a structural power shift that A did not specifically anticipate. A also did not flag the ICJ Myanmar ruling as a potential story, nor the specific UK/Australia sanctions package, nor the economy beating forecasts (Nvidia-driven growth). The 'surprises to watch' section was creative but mostly did not materialize (no hostage deal, no earthquake, no Houthi hit on a city). Overall, A captured the texture of the week well but framed the political story one level below what actually happened: it saw the arguments and the talks, not the institutional power grab.
judged.reading_b: Forecast B captured the week's political arc more accurately. Its framing of 'a visible scramble' in the Knesset, 'weakening Netanyahu's grip on power,' and the opposition gaining ground to 'undo Netanyahu's agenda' closely mirrors the actual outcome: the speaker election, the opposition's immediate legislative offensive, and the unraveling of Netanyahu's party's 'stolen election' claims. The 55-to-60 percent no-government probability was well calibrated. B correctly identified the ceasefire as under stress and the Board of Peace as a central diplomatic actor, both of which dominated coverage. The 'European and diplomatic friction' section, while not naming the UK and Australia specifically, captured the right category of event (Western sanctions on settlement-linked firms) more accurately than A's narrower French/EU framing. The winter humanitarian crisis, the Iran lobbying story, the West Bank settler violence, and the Nations League cultural friction all arrived as B described. B's 'less-likely surprise' of a limited Israeli or US strike on an Iranian target was close to the spy chief's lobbying for joint strikes, though no actual strike landed. B missed the specific ground operation (hedged as 'major,' and the actual one was 'rare and limited'), the ICJ Myanmar ruling, the Tim Hortons data controversy, and the 'Gaza Syndrome' soldier-trauma narrative. B also did not specifically predict the speaker election, but its broader framing of the opposition consolidating power and attacking Netanyahu's legislative legacy is a closer description of what the speaker election enabled than A's focus on coalition talks. B's Lebanon section (talks, wheat crop disruption) was less central to the actual week than the forecasts suggested, and the Houthi third-attack prediction did not clearly materialize. Overall, B's picture of the week as a political power shift combined with a stressed ceasefire and Western diplomatic pressure is a more accurate composite of what actually happened.
judged.comparison: Both forecasts are strong and capture the major themes: continued Gaza strikes, winter humanitarian crisis, Board of Peace pressure, US political friction, Iran tensions, West Bank settler violence, and no full government. Both correctly hedged the ground operation as unlikely (for a 'full-scale' or 'major' offensive), and the actual limited incursion on November 18 sits in the gap between their 'probable' and 'unlikely' buckets. The key differentiator is the political story. A framed it as a process: coalition talks, public spats, a possible framework announcement. B framed it as a trajectory: Netanyahu weakening, the opposition gaining institutional power, a visible scramble. The actual week delivered the latter: the speaker election was a structural power shift, not a coalition negotiation. B's language ('weakening Netanyahu's grip,' 'opposition gains ground in bid to undo Netanyahu's agenda') maps more directly onto the headlines than A's 'coalition-building talks with Arab parties.' On the sanctions story, A's specific call of 'French or EU sanctions triggered by the Melenchon ban' was a creative but partially wrong guess; B's broader 'European and diplomatic friction' section, which mentioned UK sanctions and BDS pressure, more accurately brackets the actual UK and Australia settlement sanctions. B's probability calibration (55-60 percent no government) is more useful to a reader than A's qualitative 'almost certain / probable / possible / unlikely' ladder, because the week's political outcome was genuinely uncertain and B acknowledged that uncertainty more honestly. A's strength is its specific, testable calls (the unity government push, the personal clash, the Hamilton visit), several of which hit. B's strength is that its overall composite picture, read as a whole, is a more accurate description of the week that actually unfolded. Neither forecast predicted the ICJ Myanmar ruling, the Tim Hortons controversy, or the economy beating forecasts, but these are smaller stories. On the three dominant stories of the week (ground operation, speaker election, Western sanctions), B's framing is closer to the actual events on two of the three. VERDICT: B

measurement.happened:
This week in Ukraine was dominated by the resumption of peace talks after a nine-month silence, a provocative US territorial proposal, a satellite-internet controversy, and a brutal exchange of strikes on infrastructure. Let me walk through each theme.

PEACE TALKS AND THE DONBAS-FOR-NATO PROPOSAL. The single biggest story of the week is the US-brokered round of Russia-Ukraine talks in Abu Dhabi, held November 9-11, the first in nine months. US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner mediated. The talks ended with an agreement on what Kushner called the 'largest prisoner exchange' of the war, but no breakthrough on territory or a ceasefire. Russia and Ukraine discussed a post-war European security framework, ceasefire monitoring, and territory. Then, on November 14, Zelensky dropped a bombshell: the US had floated the idea that Ukraine could cede the Donbas to Russia in exchange for guaranteed NATO membership. Zelensky said he was ready to put a NATO security deal to a referendum. He also warned that Ukraine is 'not real estate' and that the new European security framework floated by the US could benefit Putin. Trump said the US is seeing a 'strong inclination' to end the war. Rubio said Ukraine must never again feel threatened. (Sources: Reuters, AP, AFP, BBC, CNN, DW, Bloomberg, WSJ, FT, CNBC, Al Jazeera, TV5Monde.)

EUROPEAN PARTICIPATION AND INTERNAL SQUABBLING. A major sub-thread was Europe trying to get a seat at the table. The EU settled on a five-nation group of national security aides to represent Europe in future talks. There was visible internal tension: Germany's Merz demanded all EU states back Ukraine and was accused of 'blackmail' by Slovak PM Fico over linking Ukraine funding to the EU budget. Berlin and Paris initially temporized on who to send. Russia initially resisted European participation, then Putin let Europe join if they showed 'readiness to contribute.' Zelensky welcomed the prospect. Kushner said the US cannot reach a deal without Europe. The EU also agreed to present a new Russia sanctions package and Ukraine funding measures by year-end. Canada and the EU launched a new alliance covering Ukraine, minerals, and AI. (Sources: Reuters, AP, DW, Bloomberg, FT, CNBC, Al Jazeera, TV5Monde.)

STARLINK AND STARSHIELD CONTROVERSY. This was a recurring and increasingly bitter thread. Zelensky said Starshield speed limits were imposed again, hampering Ukraine's frontline defenses. He escalated his criticism of SpaceX. Democratic US senators ordered Elon Musk to preserve all records on Ukraine Starlink access. BT in the UK held off its Starlink launch until the Ukraine 'noise' died down. Ukraine's military said Starlink disruptions were recurring. This is becoming a political issue inside the US, not just a technical one. (Sources: Reuters, AP, DW, Bloomberg, WSJ, FT, CNBC, TV5Monde.)

RUSSIAN STRIKES ON UKRAINE'S INFRASTRUCTURE. Russia launched a massive overnight strike on Ukrainian military factories, hit energy facilities in eight regions, targeted food factories, and pounded the power grid. Kyiv suffered water shortages. The grid operator reported widespread damage. Ukraine raced to repair power plants before winter. Workers at a devastated power plant refused to leave. BBC joined a unit protecting a front-line city under constant drone threat. A 'horrific' Russian drone strike killed 14 at a train station. Zelensky warned Russia's strikes aim to cut Ukraine in half. (Sources: Reuters, AP, BBC, DW, Bloomberg, FT, Al Jazeera, TV5Monde.)

UKRAINE'S DRONE CAMPAIGN AGAINST RUSSIA. Ukraine launched nearly 1,200 drones at Russia in a single night. It hit a ninth Russian oil refinery since the start of November, including Russia's biggest refinery in Siberia. It struck an oil-pumping station in Samara. A drone attack triggered a fire at the Baltic port of Ust-Luga. A Ukrainian drone hit a Russian warship in the Gulf of Finland, prompting Finland to contact Ukraine. Sources say recent Ukrainian attacks have reduced Russia's oil processing capacity by 30 percent. Russia's diesel exports dropped. Russia began rationing petrol. The Russian economy is slowing as Ukrainian attacks damage industry. (Sources: Reuters, AP, BBC, DW, Bloomberg, FT, Al Jazeera, CNBC, TV5Monde.)

US ENVOYS SHUTTLE BETWEEN MOSCOW AND DUBLIN. After the Abu Dhabi talks, Witkoff and Kushner flew to Moscow to meet Putin, then to Dublin to meet Zelensky. Putin was described as inflexible and uncompromising, upping his demands. Zelensky said he was pleased with messages from the US envoys and that progress hinges on the US approach to Russia. Witkoff said progress is being made. A Zelensky-Putin direct meeting still appears unlikely at this stage. (Sources: Reuters, AP, AFP, BBC, CNN, DW, Bloomberg, FT, Al Jazeera, TV5Monde.)

RUSSIAN CASUALTIES AND THE HUMAN COST. A hacked set of official Russian statistics suggested more than 400,000 Russian troops killed. Al Jazeera reported casualties reaching 450,000. Russia recorded over 11,000 foreign military deaths. Ukraine claimed a record 3,000 Russian casualties in a single day. A mother's campaign for Ukrainian sons captured by Russia was profiled. (Sources: TV5Monde, Al Jazeera, Bloomberg, BBC.)

CAR BOMBINGS IN RUSSIA. Two car bombs hit Moscow in two days. One killed a military officer, the other badly injured a former aide to a pro-Kremlin Ukrainian ex-PM. This looks like a tit-for-tat or intelligence-driven escalation. (Sources: Reuters, AP, BBC, DW, CNN, Al Jazeera, TV5Monde.)

INDIA AND THE BLACK SEA. Zelensky spoke to Modi. India signaled readiness to mediate Black Sea food corridors. India also spoke with both Russia and Ukraine ahead of the talks. (Sources: Reuters, DW, Bloomberg, Al Jazeera, TV5Monde.)

DEFENSE TECH AND ECONOMY. Ukrainian drone startup UForce closed a $700 million funding round at a $6 billion valuation. A Ukrainian army unit pioneered drone evacuations and is scaling up. Ireland and Ukraine are considering co-production of unmanned drones. Oil prices dropped more than a dollar on hopes for peace. The EU pushed for more joint borrowing to finance Ukraine. (Sources: Reuters, BBC, Bloomberg, CNBC, FT, Al Jazeera.)

CHERNOBYL AND OTHER SMALLER STORIES. Donors promised half the funding to repair the Chernobyl exclusion-zone arch. In South Africa, police arrested nine then a tenth foreigner over an alleged plan to fight in the war. A 10th suspect was arrested. (Sources: TV5Monde, AP, BBC.)

LESS LIKELY SURPRISES. Zelensky calling a snap referendum on the NATO-Donbas deal within this week (possible but rushed). Comparing the two photographs five days apart, the most dramatic growth is in the peace-talks thread. On November 9 it was still in the preparation stage: delegations confirmed, Melania hosting, Trump calling the prospective deal 'big and beautiful.' By November 14 the talks had actually happened (November 9-11 in Abu Dhabi), produced the largest prisoner exchange of the war, and then exploded into the Donbas-for-NATO revelation that Zelensky dropped on the 14th. The theme went from anticipation to execution to a specific, controversial territorial proposal in five days. That is the single biggest shift.

Ukraine's drone campaign against Russian refineries grew sharply. The first photo recorded six refineries hit in a week. The second photo records nearly 1,200 drones launched in a single night, a ninth refinery struck (including Russia's largest in Siberia), a 30 percent reduction in Russian oil-processing capacity, a Baltic port on fire, and a warship hit in the Gulf of Finland. The scale jumped from a steady campaign to what reads like an all-out economic siege.

European involvement grew in a different way. The first photo showed Europe warning about irrelevance, the G7 meeting in Paris, and Meloni criticizing the EU's disjointed approach. The second photo shows the EU having settled on a five-nation security-aid group, Germany's Merz demanding all states back Ukraine, Slovak PM Fico accusing Berlin of blackmail over the EU budget, and Russia going from resisting European participation to accepting it if Europe shows 'readiness to contribute.' The theme moved from anxiety to concrete institutional positioning, but with visible internal friction.

The Starlink/Starshield controversy appeared almost from nothing. In the first photo it was a minor footnote (Russia using its own Starlink). By the second photo Zelensky was publicly escalating his criticism of SpaceX, Democratic senators had ordered Elon Musk to preserve all records on Ukraine's Starlink access, and the British telecom BT had held off its Starlink launch until the 'noise' died down. A technical issue became a political flashpoint in the US within five days.

Russian strikes on Ukrainian infrastructure continued and evolved. The first photo focused on power substations, a bridge, and the deadly aid-center strike in Zaporizhzhia. The second photo shows strikes on military factories, energy facilities in eight regions, food factories, the power grid, and a train station where 14 were killed. Kyiv now has water shortages. The pattern is the same (overnight barrages, energy focus) but the targets have broadened to include industry and food processing, and the cumulative damage is becoming visible in daily life.

Several themes shrank or vanished. The Kherson ceasefire ending was a specific event in the first photo and is no longer in the news by the second. The Zelensky-mayor blame game over the blackout was a one-off and disappeared. The SBU corruption scandal, prominent on November 9, is barely visible by November 14. The IMF review, launched on the 9th, has faded from the headlines. Melania Trump's role as 'exclusive intermediary' was central in the first photo and is much quieter in the second.

New themes that appeared between the two photos: the Donbas-for-NATO proposal (the biggest new item), two car bombings in Moscow within two days, India signaling readiness to mediate Black Sea food corridors, the US envoys Witkoff and Kushner physically shuttling to Moscow and then Dublin, the UForce drone startup closing a 700-million-dollar round at a 6-billion valuation, and the Canadian-EU alliance covering Ukraine, minerals, and AI. The car bombings in particular are new: the first photo had no mention of car bombs on Russian soil.

The overall speed of change is fast. The diplomatic track moved from preparation to talks to a specific territorial proposal in five days. The economic-war track went from six refineries to nine and a 30 percent capacity hit. The Starlink issue went from footnote to congressional order. These are not slow drifts; they are step-changes compressed into a weekend and a few working days.

They produced the largest prisoner exchange of the war, which counts as a tangible outcome but is narrower than the 'framework document' I predicted. No full ceasefire, as expected. What I got wrong: the talks themselves did not produce the Donbas-for-NATO proposal. That came on November 14, after the talks, as a revelation by Zelensky about what the US had floated. I expected the talks to center on 'security guarantees and the scope of any ceasefire.' They did, but the specific shape of the US position (cede Donbas, get NATO) was more concrete and more provocative than my 'friction over security guarantees' framing suggested. The talks also produced a post-war European security framework discussion and a ceasefire-monitoring conversation, which I did not specifically predict.

Russian strikes on energy. Expected: almost certain, at least one major overnight barrage, hundreds of thousands without power. Reality: fully confirmed and then some. The overnight strike hit military factories, energy in eight regions, food factories, and the grid. Kyiv had water shortages. Fourteen people were killed at a train station. Workers at a devastated power plant refused to leave. This came true exactly as predicted, maybe slightly more broadly in target types (food factories, military plants) than I specified.

Ukraine's refinery campaign. Expected: probable, at least one or two more strikes on refineries or logistics. Reality: massively exceeded expectations. Nearly 1,200 drones in one night, the ninth refinery of November, Russia's largest refinery in Siberia hit, an oil-pumping station in Samara struck, the Baltic port of Ust-Luga on fire, a warship hit in the Gulf of Finland, and a reported 30 percent reduction in Russian oil-processing capacity. I said 'one or two more strikes.' It was closer to a sustained campaign with a dramatic nighttime surge. I underestimated the tempo and the geographic spread.

Post-talks diplomatic scramble. Expected: almost certain, a flurry of statements from Trump, Zelensky, Putin, Meloni, Merz, Kallas. Reality: yes, but more substantive than a 'flurry of statements.' The US envoys physically traveled to Moscow and Dublin. The EU settled on a five-nation security group. Merz and Fico had a public spat over the EU budget. Russia went from resisting to accepting European participation. The Donbas-for-NATO proposal was revealed. Trump said the US sees a 'strong inclination' to end the war. Rubio said Ukraine must never again feel threatened. This was more than statements; it was institutional positioning and a specific policy proposal. I was right that it would be active but wrong about the form.

IMF review. Expected: probable that the review is underway, almost certain not concluded. Reality: the IMF is barely mentioned in the second photo. The review is presumably ongoing but has not generated headlines. I overestimated its news salience for this specific week. The process is moving, but it is not a driver of this week's story.

Winter heating crisis. Expected: probable, growing complaints, possible rationing, public appeals. Reality: confirmed. Kyiv water shortages, grid operator reporting widespread damage, Ukraine racing to repair before winter, workers refusing to leave a devastated plant. The crisis is real and visible. I was right.

Cyber incidents. Expected: possible, at least one more notable incident. Reality: the 400,000-casualty figure is still circulating (now 450,000 per Al Jazeera), but the alert-app hacking and fake nuclear warnings are no longer prominent. The cyber thread has faded somewhat as a standalone news item, though the casualty-data leak persists. Partially true, but less active than expected.

European military preparation. Expected: probable that exercises continue, unlikely a full deployment decision. Reality: the multinational exercise is not specifically mentioned in the second photo. Instead, the European thread is dominated by the five-nation security group, the Merz-Fico budget fight, and the Canada-EU alliance. The military-exercise angle has been overtaken by the diplomatic-institutional angle. I was right that groundwork is being laid but wrong about the specific form it takes this week.

Domestic political friction. Expected: possible, one more spat or minor reshuffle. Reality: the SBU corruption scandal and the Zelensky-mayor blame game are much quieter in the second photo. The domestic friction has not escalated as I tentatively predicted. It has receded from the headlines. I was too pessimistic (or too attentive to a one-off) about this thread.

US congressional dynamics. Expected: probable, new Congress makes noise, possibly about Patriot systems. Reality: yes, but in a different form. Democratic senators ordered Elon Musk to preserve all records on Ukraine's Starlink access. This is the new Congress acting, but on Starlink rather than on Patriot systems or a structured aid package. I was right that the Congress would be active but wrong about the specific issue.

Things that came that were not expected: the Donbas-for-NATO proposal was the biggest surprise. I expected 'security guarantees' to be discussed but not a specific territorial concession tied to NATO membership. The two car bombings in Moscow in two days were not in my 'less likely surprises' list (I had a Ukrainian drone or missile strike on a Russian capital, which is different from car bombs). India's mediation role on Black Sea food corridors was not mentioned at all in my expectations. The Starlink controversy escalating to a US congressional order was not anticipated. The UForce 700-million-dollar funding round and the Ireland-Ukraine drone co-production were not expected. The warship hit in the Gulf of Finland, prompting Finland to contact Ukraine, was not in my list.

What this says about how our expectations have been wrong for Ukraine: the main pattern is underestimating the specificity and boldness of the US diplomatic position. I expected a framework discussion on security guarantees. The US actually proposed a concrete territorial trade (Donbas for NATO). The second pattern is underestimating the tempo of Ukraine's economic-war campaign. I said 'one or two more strikes.' It was a 1,200-drone night and a 30 percent capacity hit. The third pattern is overestimating the salience of slower-moving institutional processes (IMF review, military exercises) and underestimating the speed at which technical issues (Starlink) become political flashpoints. The fourth pattern is underestimating the role of third parties (India, Canada) and intra-European friction (Merz-Fico) as independent news drivers. In short, my expectations were too institutional and too gradual. The actual week was more dramatic, more specific, and more multi-actor than I modeled.
delta.driver: The force pushing Ukraine from the first photograph to the second is the collision between American urgency to close the war and the gap between what Russia wants on the ground and what Ukraine will accept in exchange. The US midterms are done, the new Democratic Congress is seated and already acting, and Trump wants a 'big and beautiful' deal before the political window shifts again. That urgency is translating into a specific, provocative proposal (cede the Donbas, get NATO) that neither side has fully accepted but both are now negotiating around. At the same time, both belligerents are using maximum kinetic pressure as leverage in the same window: Russia is hitting energy, food, and military industry to make Ukraine feel the winter and the war before it signs, and Ukraine is hitting refineries, ports, and a warship to make Russia feel the economic squeeze before it negotiates from strength. The Starlink controversy is the clearest symptom of this collision: the US controls a critical piece of Ukraine's warfighting infrastructure, and both the political pressure to close the deal and the military pressure to keep fighting are now being fought over satellite bandwidth. Europe is trying to insert itself into this three-way pressure before it is sidelined, which adds a fourth vector of influence (and friction) to an already crowded diplomatic space. The net effect is that five days of headlines in Ukraine are driven less by any single battlefield event than by the accelerating convergence of a US-deadline, a Russian territorial demand, a Ukrainian security demand, and a European institutional anxiety, all compressing into the same short window.

crystal.reasoning:
I start from the present: the Donbas-for-NATO proposal was dropped on Saturday, November 14, the very first day of the forecast window. Zelensky said he is ready to put a NATO security deal to a referendum. The US envoys are still in transit between Moscow and Dublin. Russia has just hit energy, food, and military industry in eight regions. Ukraine just launched 1,200 drones and hit a ninth refinery. Starlink has gone from technical footnote to a US congressional order. The EU has a five-nation group but is still squabbling. India is circling the Black Sea. Two car bombs hit Moscow in two days. This is a week that opens at maximum diplomatic and kinetic tension.

The motion tells me the diplomatic track is accelerating, not decelerating. Five days ago the talks were in preparation; now they are in the 'specific proposal being debated' phase. The next logical step is not another round of talks but the reaction to the proposal: who accepts, who rejects, who conditions, who threatens to walk. The motion also shows Ukraine's economic-war tempo is climbing, not plateauing. Nine refineries in a month, 30 percent capacity loss, a warship hit, a Baltic port on fire. The next week will likely see the campaign continue at that tempo or higher, because Ukraine has momentum and Russia has not yet shown a visible counter to the drone swarm. The Starlink thread is in its escalation phase: it went from footnote to congressional order in five days. The next step is either a partial resolution (Musk restores access with conditions) or a further political escalation (a hearing, a formal inquiry, a US government position). The European thread is in its 'institutional positioning' phase: the five-nation group exists on paper, the Merz-Fico budget fight is live, the sanctions package is being drafted. The next step is the first real coordination meeting and the first public disagreement about scope.

The wind tells me I have been wrong in four specific ways, and I must correct. First, I underweight the specificity and boldness of the US position. I should not say 'the US will press for security guarantees.' I should say 'the US will push the Donbas-for-NATO trade as a concrete package and demand a yes-or-no response.' Second, I underweight the tempo of Ukraine's economic war. I should not say 'one or two more refinery strikes.' I should expect the 1,200-drone night to be the new baseline, not the peak. Third, I overweight slow institutional processes. The IMF review, the EU sanctions drafting, the five-nation group's first meeting are real but will not be the headline. The headline will be the referendum debate, the next Russian barrage, and the next Ukrainian drone night. Fourth, I underweight third parties and technical-to-political escalation. India will do something concrete on the Black Sea. Starlink will generate a specific US political event, not just 'more discussion.' The Merz-Fico fight will produce a specific budget consequence, not just 'tension.'

The driver is the same as last week but compressed: the US wants a deal before the political window shifts, Russia wants to extract maximum territory before the winter makes Ukraine desperate, Ukraine wants to hit Russia's economy hard enough that Russia negotiates from weakness, and Europe wants a seat before it is written out. The referendum idea is the new accelerant: it gives Zelensky a way to accept the Donbas concession without looking like he is giving it away, but it also gives every Ukrainian opposition faction, every pro-war general, and every European leader a reason to either support or attack the proposal within days. That is what will drive the news cycle this week.

What I would not bet on: a Zelensky-Putin face-to-face meeting (the shuttle diplomacy is not ready for that), a full ceasefire (the kinetic pressure is too high and the proposal too fresh), a major Ukrainian ground offensive (the energy crisis is consuming resources), a Russian nuclear statement (no trigger), a Ukrainian government reshuffle (the referendum debate will absorb domestic politics), a formal US congressional vote on a new aid package (the Starlink fight is eating the Congress's bandwidth), a new front opening in the Black Sea with a naval engagement (India and Turkey are mediating, not fighting), and a major cyberattack of the alert-app scale (the novelty has worn off).
crystal.forecast:
THE DONBAS-FOR-NATO REFERENDUM DEBATE. This will dominate the week. Zelensky dropped the proposal on Saturday; Monday through Friday will be consumed by reactions. I expect Zelensky to clarify the referendum's scope and timing, likely framing it as a 30-to-60-day process that would cover both the territorial concession and the NATO membership guarantee as a single package. The Ukrainian opposition, particularly the pro-war factions and the regional governors of Donbas oblasts, will mobilize within 48 hours, calling the referendum either a premature capitulation or a necessary test of the nation's will. Russia will issue a statement welcoming the 'pragmatic approach' while quietly demanding that the referendum also cover the status of the Crimean peninsula and the language of the NATO guarantee. Trump will make at least one public statement urging both sides to say yes before the winter deepens. The European five-nation group will issue a joint statement, likely split between those who love the NATO part and those who worry the territorial concession sets a precedent. I am confident this will be the single biggest story of the week. The less-likely surprise the motion makes more probable: Zelensky actually setting a specific date for the referendum, say mid-December, which would force all other threads to organize around that deadline.

RUSSIAN KINETIC ESCALATION AND WINTER PRESSURE. Russia will launch at least one more major overnight barrage, and the pattern will continue to broaden. Last week the targets were energy, food factories, military plants, and a train station. I expect this week to see strikes on water infrastructure (Kyiv already has shortages), possibly a chemical or pharmaceutical plant, and at least one strike on a railway hub or a bridge that was not hit last week. The winter heating crisis will worsen: I expect at least one major city to report a full-day power outage, public queues for heating fuel, and Zelensky making a direct appeal to the population to conserve. The less-likely surprise: a Russian strike that hits a major hospital or a school, generating a new wave of international outrage and possibly a UN Security Council emergency session. I would not bet on a Russian ground offensive in this window; the kinetic pressure is coming from the air, not the front.

UKRAINE'S DRONE AND ECONOMIC CAMPAIGN. The 1,200-drone night and the 30 percent capacity reduction are the new baseline, not the peak. I expect Ukraine to hit at least one more refinery or oil-processing facility, and to expand the target set to include a second warship or a naval base in the Black Sea or the Baltic. The Samara pumping station and the Ust-Luga port fire suggest Ukraine is hitting the logistics chain, not just the processing plants. I expect a strike on a major railway junction or a pipeline terminal. Russia's petrol rationing will spread to at least two more regions. The less-likely surprise: a Ukrainian drone or missile hitting a target inside Moscow or St. Petersburg, not just the suburbs, which would be a step up in the tit-for-tat escalation that the car bombings have set in motion. I am moderately confident in the continued refinery campaign and the expansion to logistics; less confident in a Moscow-centre hit, but the car-bomb pattern makes it more probable than it looks.

STARLINK AND THE US POLITICAL BATTLE. The congressional order to preserve records is the floor, not the ceiling. I expect at least one of three things: a formal hearing or subcommittee session where Musk or a SpaceX executive is questioned, a US State Department or Pentagon statement clarifying the government's position on Ukraine's Starlink access, or a partial restoration of Starlink service with new conditions that Zelensky publicly accepts or rejects. The British BT launch decision will be revisited, either going ahead or being delayed again. Fire Point and other Ukrainian alternatives will get a new funding announcement or a government contract. The less-likely surprise: a Republican senator or the White House itself taking a public position, which would turn the Starlink issue from a Democratic-leaned congressional fight into a broader US political story. I am confident the Starlink thread will generate at least one major news event this week; the specific form is uncertain.

EUROPEAN INSTITUTIONAL POSITIONING AND THE MERZ-FICO FIGHT. The five-nation security group will hold its first coordination meeting or produce its first joint position paper. The Merz-Fico budget fight will either produce a specific compromise (Ukraine funding linked to a timeline) or a public deadlock that stalls the EU sanctions package. The new Russia sanctions package will be in its drafting or voting stage, with at least one member state (likely Hungary or Slovakia) pushing for a watered-down version. The Canada-EU alliance will produce a concrete first deliverable, possibly a joint statement on mineral supply chains or a specific AI collaboration project. I am moderately confident in the five-nation group producing something visible; less confident in the sanctions package being finalized, because the Merz-Fico fight is a real obstacle.

US ENVOY SHUTTLE AND THE PUSH FOR A RESPONSE. Witkoff and Kushner will make at least one more trip to Moscow and one to Kyiv or Dublin. The purpose will be to get Russia and Ukraine to respond to the Donbas-for-NATO proposal. I expect Putin to be described as 'inflexible' or 'studying the proposal' and Zelensky to be described as 'open but demanding guarantees.' A Zelensky-Putin direct phone call is possible but I would not bet on it; the shuttle diplomacy is the preferred channel. Trump will make at least one public statement, likely on social media, expressing optimism or mild frustration. The less-likely surprise: the US envoys presenting a written 'package deal' that bundles the Donbas concession, the NATO guarantee, the ceasefire monitoring mechanism, and the prisoner-exchange framework into a single document, which would be a step beyond last week's 'discussion' phase.

INDIA, THE BLACK SEA, AND THIRD-PARTY MEDIATION. India's signal of readiness to mediate Black Sea food corridors will produce a concrete next step: a joint India-Ukraine-Russia working group, a specific corridor proposal, or a statement from Modi's office. Turkey will be drawn in as the strait authority. I expect at least one grain or fuel shipment to transit the Black Sea under a new or updated framework. The less-likely surprise: India formally proposing to host a follow-up round of talks, which would be a significant shift in the diplomatic geography.

RUSSIAN DOMESTIC PRESSURE: CAR BOMBS, CASUALTIES, AND PUBLIC OPINION. The two car bombs in Moscow in two days will generate a security crackdown and possibly a third incident. Russian authorities will announce a 'major operation' or an arrest wave. The 400,000-to-450,000 casualty figure will continue to circulate, and Russia will either confirm a revised number or release a contradictory figure. I expect at least one Russian regional governor to publicly complain about the war's economic impact, which would be a sign of internal pressure. The less-likely surprise: a visible protest or a low-level official resignation in a Russian city, which would signal that the war's domestic cost is starting to register in public life.

UKRAINIAN DOMESTIC POLITICS AND THE REFERENDUM BACKLASH. The referendum idea will trigger internal debate. I expect the opposition to hold at least one rally or issue a joint statement, the regional governors of Donetsk and Luhansk to publicly weigh in, and the SBU or the military to issue a statement supporting or questioning the timing. Zelensky's approval ratings will be discussed in the media, and at least one poll will be released. I would not bet on a government reshuffle or a no-confidence motion in this window; the referendum debate will absorb the domestic political energy.

ECONOMY, OIL, AND FINANCE. Oil prices will be volatile: the peace-talks optimism will pull prices down, while the refinery damage and petrol rationing will pull them up. I expect a net decline of 1 to 3 percent over the week, with a spike if a major refinery is hit. Ukraine's sovereign bonds will react to the referendum news: a short-term dip on the territorial-concession fear, followed by a recovery if the NATO guarantee is seen as credible. The EU's joint borrowing mechanism for Ukraine will see a new tranche discussion or a specific allocation. The UForce funding round will be followed by at least one more Ukrainian defense-tech deal or partnership announcement.
crystal.headline: Ukraine Weighs Donbas Referendum as Drone War Intensifies
emoji_reasons: Zelensky's proposal to put the Donbas-for-NATO trade to a public referendum is the single most consequential and new development of the week, reshaping the entire diplomatic and domestic political landscape.

Both sides are escalating kinetic pressure simultaneously: Russia is broadening its strikes to food, water, and military industry, while Ukraine is hitting refineries, ports, and warships at a tempo that is becoming a sustained economic siege.

The Starlink controversy has escalated from a technical dispute to a US congressional order, making satellite internet access a political flashpoint that will generate at least one major news event in the coming days.
crystal.tldr: Next week will be dominated by the fallout from the US Donbas-for-NATO proposal and Zelensky's referendum idea, with both sides and Europe reacting in the first 48 hours. Russia will continue its overnight barrages on energy, water, and food infrastructure as winter deepens, while Ukraine will push its drone campaign against Russian refineries and logistics at the new high tempo. The Starlink dispute will escalate into a specific US political event, and the EU will struggle to present a unified position amid the Merz-Fico budget fight.
crystal.eli5:
Imagine a big argument between three friends about how to split a pizza. One friend (the US) just said, "You can give them a slice of your pizza, but in return, you get to sit at the table at every dinner party forever." The other two friends (Ukraine and Russia) are now arguing about whether that deal is fair. Ukraine's leader said he wants to ask all his friends (the voters) what they think before he agrees. That is the referendum idea. It is the biggest story this week.

At the same time, both sides are still throwing things at each other. Russia is hitting Ukraine's power plants, water pipes, and food factories, trying to make winter really hard so Ukraine will say yes to the deal. Ukraine is sending thousands of small flying robots (drones) at Russia's oil factories, trying to make Russia's gas stations run dry so Russia will also say yes. Both sides are using their strongest moves right now because they think the window to make a deal is closing.

There is also a side-argument about the internet. Ukraine uses a special satellite internet system to talk to its soldiers, and the company that runs it has been slowing it down. Now the US politicians are getting angry and ordering the company to keep all its records. It is like if your school's Wi-Fi kept getting slow during a test, and the principal started asking the internet company for a full report.

Europe is trying to get a seat at the pizza-splitting table, but they are arguing among themselves about who gets to speak for the whole group. India is offering to help fix the delivery route for grain ships in the Black Sea. And in Russia, two car bombs went off in the capital in two days, which makes the government nervous and the public more impatient about the war.

emoji_reasons: The resumption of US-brokered peace talks in Abu Dhabi, the Donbas-for-NATO proposal, and the push to include Europe in negotiations made diplomacy the defining story of the week.

Russia pounded Ukraine's power grid, water supply, and military factories while Ukraine hit nine Russian refineries and a warship, making the exchange of strikes on infrastructure the constant backdrop.

The Starlink and Starshield speed-limit controversy, Zelensky's public escalation against SpaceX, and the US congressional order for Musk to preserve records turned a satellite-internet issue into a major political and military story.

judged.reading_a: Forecast A hit on a large share of the week's actual events, and its extra specificity often paid off. The Russian kinetic-escalation section was well calibrated: it expected a major overnight barrage, strikes on water infrastructure, a major city reporting power outages, and Zelensky appealing for conservation. The actual week delivered a massive November 20 barrage on Kyiv that damaged two bridges, knocked out water and power, and hit the Dutch and Austrian embassies, followed by a ballistic missile on Kryvyi Rih that killed a seven-year-old and an emergency worker. A's framing of the winter heating crisis and public conservation appeal was directionally right even if the specific 'queues for heating fuel' detail was not a headline. The drone-and-economic section was A's strongest military call: it expected Ukraine to hit at least one more refinery, to expand the target set to a naval or Black Sea/Baltic target, and to strike a major railway junction or pipeline terminal as part of a broader 'logistics chain' campaign. The actual week saw Ukraine hit refineries in Krasnodar and Tatarstan, more Russian regions limit fuel sales, and, most dramatically, partially collapse the Kerch Bridge in a 1,300-drone barrage. A's 'logistics chain' framing is the closest either forecast came to capturing that bridge strike, even though A listed it under 'railway junction or pipeline terminal' rather than naming the bridge. The Starlink section was specific and largely right: A expected a formal hearing, a State Department or Pentagon statement, or a partial restoration with conditions. The actual week brought a public Zelensky-Musk clash, Musk accusing Zelensky of lying, and Trump's intelligence chief warning that no SpaceX funding would flow without answers. A's 'less likely surprise' of a Republican senator or the White House taking a public position was close to the intel-chief intervention. The European institutional section got the five-nation coordination meeting right (the Berlin 'Coalition of the Willing' summit on November 19) and the EU loan right (the 45 billion euro proposal, partly serviced by Russian frozen-asset profits). A's 'less likely surprise' of Zelensky setting a specific referendum date did not quite materialize; he said he was 'ready to put a NATO security deal to a referendum' but did not pin down a mid-December date. The US envoy shuttle section was partially right: Witkoff and Kushner were expected in Berlin, and Trump made multiple public statements. But A's framing of 'shuttle diplomacy' as the preferred channel undersold the actual event, which was Trump personally meeting Putin at the APEC summit in a trilateral setting with Xi. A's 'Zelensky-Putin direct phone call is possible but I would not bet on it' was conservative; the trilateral summit was a bigger step than either a phone call or an envoy shuttle. The India-Black Sea thread was A's weakest call: it expected a joint working group, a corridor proposal, or a Modi office statement, none of which appeared as a headline this week. The Russian domestic pressure section expected a security crackdown after the car bombs and a regional governor complaining about economic impact; the car bombs were last week's news and the crackdown was not a headline this week, though Bloomberg's piece on Putin's war ravaging a generation of Russian men fits the broader theme. The Ukrainian domestic politics section expected an opposition rally, regional governors weighing in, and a poll release; these were not the dominant domestic stories, which were instead the referendum debate and the reaction to the Trump-Putin meeting. The economy-and-finance section was directionally right on the EU loan and defense-tech deals (Germany backing Auterion and Skyfall, the UK pledging over 1,000 missiles), though the specific oil-price prediction of a 1-to-3 percent net decline was not a headline. Overall, A's picture was comprehensive and captured most of the week's major threads, with the referendum debate as the anchor. Its main overreach was rating the referendum as 'the single biggest story of the week' when the Crimean Bridge strike and the Trump-Putin-Xi summit were arguably bigger. Its main misses were the India thread, the specific domestic-politics events, and the exact diplomatic format (summit rather than shuttle).
judged.reading_b: Forecast B was more focused and made fewer, more confident predictions, and most of them came true. The Donbas-for-NATO section was directionally right: B expected Zelensky to consult his cabinet and hint at or schedule a referendum, and he did say he was ready to put the deal to a vote. B expected Putin to use the proposal to pressure Kyiv while downplaying it; the actual week saw Russia rejecting formal NATO membership (Ryabkov) while Kushner said Russia was 'comfortable' with NATO-like guarantees, which is a more nuanced response than B's 'downplaying' framing but in the same spirit. B rated this 'almost certain' as the dominant headline cluster, which is an overstatement given the Bridge and the summit were bigger, but it was certainly a top-three story. The second-round-talks section was B's best diplomatic call: it expected either a second round of trilateral talks or preparatory bilateral meetings. The actual event was the Trump-Putin-Xi trilateral at APEC, which is closer to B's 'trilateral talks' framing than to A's 'shuttle diplomacy.' B's 'probable' rating for a second formal round was well calibrated, even if the format (APEC summit hosted by Xi) was beyond what either forecast specified. The prisoner-exchange prediction was B's clearest miss: it expected the first wave of prisoners to be exchanged within the window, with bureaucratic friction and possibly a public ceremony. None of that appeared in the headlines; the exchange was agreed in principle at Abu Dhabi but the logistics did not produce a headline event this week. The Russian strikes section was right and well calibrated at 'almost certain': continued and intensified strikes on energy and water, more blackouts in Kyiv, the 'toughest winter' framing becoming daily reality. The actual barrage on November 20 and the Kryvyi Rih missile hit on November 21 confirmed this. The drone-strikes section was right at 'probable': B expected continued strikes on refineries, pipelines, and storage, with a possible new high-profile strike. The Krasnodar and Tatarstan refinery hits and the spreading fuel rationing confirmed this, though B's framing was narrower than A's 'logistics chain' and did not point toward the Bridge. The Starlink section was right at 'probable': B expected Musk or SpaceX to respond publicly, the US government to intervene, and a possible small political firestorm. The actual Zelensky-Musk clash, the 'lying' accusation, and the Trump intel-chief warning all fit. B's 'probable' rating was well calibrated. The EU budget section was partially right: B expected more public sparring between Germany and eastern EU states and a draft funding package to be tabled. The 45 billion euro loan was tabled, but the Merz-Fico sparring was not the dominant EU story this week; the Berlin summit and the 'Yalta 2.0' optics were bigger. measurement.happened:
This week in North Korea was dominated by three intertwined stories: a massive cyber-crypto heist, a symbolic break from the past via a flag redesign, and continued military and diplomatic posturing.

The biggest story by far was the aftermath of what multiple outlets describe as a roughly six-billion-dollar heist carried out by North Korean hackers against Binance, one of the world's largest cryptocurrency exchanges. The Washington Post (via WSJ) reported that the US Department of Justice helped freeze nearly half of the stolen funds, while Bloomberg noted the US detailed a 2.7-billion-dollar freeze specifically tied to the Binance hack. The BBC and Deutsche Welle added a second layer: the FBI said North Korean hackers used fake video calls to pull off a 400-million-dollar crypto scam, suggesting a coordinated multi-pronged operation. The BBC also ran a broader piece asking whether North Korea is effectively creating a new generation of world-class hackers, framing this not as a one-off crime but as a systemic capability. In short, the world learned that North Korea's cyber apparatus is now a major financial force, and Washington is publicly showing its hand by freezing billions.

The second major theme was Kim Jong Un remaking North Korea's flag, reportedly ditching the Soviet-era design. The Wall Street Journal reported this on November 14. This is a deeply symbolic act: changing a national flag is not a small bureaucratic tweak, it is a statement of identity and a signal to both the domestic population and the outside world that Pyongyang is redefining itself. It likely ties into a broader narrative of self-reliance and a break from the old socialist bloc's visual language. Expect heavy propaganda coverage of the new flag in the days ahead.

Third, the military and diplomatic picture remained tense but static. Reuters reported that Kim personally inspected the construction of a key naval base, and Bloomberg added that North Korea plans a new torpedo deployment next year as part of a broader naval push. This suggests sustained investment in maritime power, possibly aimed at the Yellow Sea and the Sea of Japan. On the diplomatic front, Reuters noted that South Korea sees little prospect of US-North Korea contact around the APEC summit, and that North Korea accused the UN Secretary-General of siding with South Korea over border tensions. Deutsche Welle asked whether Trump-Kim talks will happen anytime soon, implying they are not imminent. The overall diplomatic mood is one of frustration and slow-burn tension rather than active negotiation.

A lighter but telling thread ran through the AP and CNN: defectors are openly discussing Kim Jong Un's daughter as a likely heir apparent, and CNN reported on a paradoxical BBQ boom in a country where meat is scarce. Together these paint a picture of a regime where succession is quietly being managed and the domestic economy shows pockets of consumer activity even amid broader scarcity.

In summary: the week was defined by the crypto-heist fallout, a symbolic flag change, ongoing naval buildup, diplomatic stagnation around APEC, and background chatter about succession and daily life.
