display.eli5:
Last week, North Korean hackers stole about six billion dollars from a big crypto company called Binance. This week, the US government froze about 2.7 billion of that stolen money, basically saying 'we found your cash and we are keeping it.' North Korea is going to be very angry about this and will put out an official statement saying the US is being a thief or a bully. You will see a lot of news stories about this, with experts explaining how the hackers used fake video calls and AI tricks to pull it off.

At the same time, Kim Jong Un is changing North Korea's flag. The old one looked a lot like the Soviet Union flag, and the new one is different. This is a big deal in a country where symbols matter a lot. Think of it like a teenager changing their profile picture to signal they are a different person now. State TV will show the new flag everywhere, and news reporters will try to figure out what it means.

On the military side, instead of launching a bunch of missiles for show, North Korea is building up its navy. Kim walked around a new naval base under construction, and they are planning to add new torpedoes next year. This is a slower, quieter kind of military spending, more like building a new garage than showing off a new car. You probably will not see a big missile launch this week, but you might see a photo of a new torpedo or a small boat exercise.

Diplomatically, things are stuck. The US and North Korea are not talking much. South Korea says a US-North Korea meeting around a big international summit is unlikely. North Korea is grumbling that the US is being too hostile and missing its chance to talk. It is the diplomatic equivalent of two people standing on the phone going 'are you still there?' without actually saying anything useful.

In the background, there is quiet chatter about whether Kim's daughter might one day take over. Defectors who left the country are talking about it, and reporters are picking up those conversations. It is not an official announcement, just a slow drift in how people outside the country are reading the family dynamics. And in a country where meat is scarce, there is somehow a boom in BBQ restaurants, which reporters are finding both funny and puzzling.

A's description of the flag entering a 'propagation phase' with state media explanation pieces and Western analytical coverage matches what the WSJ reported about Kim ditching the Soviet-era design. A correctly identified that the flag would be a statement spread across commentary rather than a single ceremony, and that no grand unveiling would headline the week. A gave the Trump-Kim meeting a 10-15 percent probability and listed it under 'what I would not bet on,' which is defensible since no meeting occurred, but the speculation itself consumed the week's headlines, and A's framing of diplomacy as mere 'grumbling' undersold the event. A's 'infrastructure register' language for the military theme is close in spirit but does not clearly encompass a confirmed facility expansion. The AI chatbot at an IT exhibition, noted by 38 North, was not in A's predictions. A's overall picture of a week of 'continuation at slightly lower volume' is roughly fair, though the diplomatic speculation was louder than 'stagnation' implies. Its expectation that the flag would feature heavily in state media and that the WSJ's Soviet-era-break framing would prompt further analysis was correct. The cyber continuation prediction was broadly right, with the BBC podcast and TV5Monde video providing the expected second wave, though B's stronger claim that North Korea would 'almost certainly respond with rhetoric through KCNA' and its rating of a 'follow-on cyber operation or at least a public threat of one as probable' were not clearly borne out in the headlines. B's 'show-of-strength mode rather than deal-making mode' framing is partially wrong because the week was actually dominated by deal-making speculation (Trump floating the meeting, Xi backing easing, Putin potentially meeting Kim), even though no deal was struck.
judged.comparison: The two forecasts are remarkably similar in structure, content, and accuracy, and they share the same major blind spots. Both correctly predicted the flag propagation, the continued cyber/hacking media cycle, the succession background noise, and the absence of a nuclear test, ICBM launch, or actual Trump-Kim meeting. Both missed the IAEA uranium-enrichment expansion finding, which was one of the week's most significant multi-outlet stories (IAEA, WSJ satellite photos, Reuters, AP, DW, Al Jazeera). measurement.happened:
This week in Venezuela was dominated by a remarkable oil investment renaissance following the political transition that saw Maduro ousted. The single most important story was the wave of major energy deals and assessments. ExxonMobil signed a preliminary agreement to assess seven areas for possible energy projects, a stunning reversal after the company had previously called the country uninvestable. Vitol landed a prized oil contract through a trader with personal ties to JD Vance, as Reuters exclusively reported. Qatar's UCC began pursuing expansion into onshore fields, Chevron's patience was paying off with visible results, and Brazil's Petrobras signaled strong interest with the energy minister heading to Caracas. Ecopetrol entered talks for a ten-year gas supply deal, and Venezuela sent its first oil gear in years to the US for repairs. The US-backed oil company even flaunted Venezuelan facilities to the world. All of this was supported by headlines from Reuters, Bloomberg, WSJ, FT, and TV5Monde.

The second major theme was the US financial management of Venezuelan oil proceeds. Multiple sources including Reuters, AP, WSJ, and Al Jazeera reported that the US had handled roughly 12 billion dollars of Venezuelan oil revenues since Maduro's ouster and returned nearly all of it. Bloomberg added that 9 billion of that went specifically to buoying the Bolivar. The US Treasury was also weighing a short-term loan to help Venezuela service its IDB debt, and the IDB board approved an engagement note for the country. This paints a picture of a Venezuela whose oil finances are effectively running through Washington, with the US acting as both manager and creditor.

The third theme was the electricity crisis and the legislative response to it. Venezuela's lawmakers passed a power law opening the crisis-hit sector to private investment, as reported by Reuters, Bloomberg, and AFP. Yet more than half of Venezuelans were facing near-daily blackouts, and the US-backed leader, identified in Bloomberg headlines as Rodriguez, was grappling with protests over the power situation. The crisis had a new front opening, as the Bloomberg Spanish headline noted. Meanwhile, construction flaws were found in housing towers that had collapsed in the recent earthquakes, adding a structural-safety dimension to the infrastructure narrative, per CNN and Deutsche Welle.

The fourth theme was broad international engagement and diplomacy. Foreign investors were heading to Caracas amid the political transition, the IDB formally re-engaged, Brazil and Venezuela vowed to upgrade ties with oil investment talks, and at COP31 the Venezuelan delegation promoted its oil while Greta Thunberg and traffic chaos made headlines. TV5Monde covered the COP31 oil push in French, noting that US aid was boosting Venezuelan oil fields. The Oxford University professor quoted by Deutsche Welle framed the earthquake as a geopolitical stress test for the interim government, underscoring that the transition is still fragile.

The fifth, smaller theme was regional border issues. Venezuela and Colombia agreed to collaborate on border security following a series of kidnappings, and Venezuela vowed to complete repairs on the Colombia pipeline by March. This suggests the two neighbors are trying to stabilize their shared border and energy infrastructure simultaneously.

crystal.eli5:
Imagine Venezuela is like a house that's been broken for a long time. The owner (Maduro) just moved out, and a new manager (Rodriguez) stepped in with a lot of help from the US. This week, a bunch of big construction companies showed up to fix the house's plumbing (the oil fields). ExxonMobil, Chevron, and five others are all trying to get a piece of the work. It's like a gold rush, but with oil rigs instead of shovels.

Here's the tricky part: the US isn't just watching. The US is actually holding the house's money. Twelve billion dollars of oil revenue went through Washington's hands, and nine billion of that was used to keep the house's currency (the Bolivar) from falling apart. Think of it like a parent managing a teenager's allowance, except the teenager is a whole country and the allowance is in oil money. Next week, the US is likely to make a bigger financial decision — maybe a loan through an international bank — that will either help the house stand up straighter or create a new argument about who's in charge.

Meanwhile, the lights still go out. More than half the people in the house can't count on the electricity working. The government just passed a new rule that lets outside companies fix the wiring, which is good in theory. But the lights are still off, and people are still angry. The new manager, Rodriguez, is going to have to deal with that anger in a visible way this week — maybe a protest, maybe a speech, maybe a trip to a neighboring country to show the world the house is being fixed.

And here's a small drama: one of the companies that got a big oil contract (Vitol) got the deal through a middleman who knows JD Vance personally. In a normal country that's just a business deal. In Venezuela, where the US is already managing the money, it looks a lot like a favor. Expect someone to ask questions about that, and for it to become a political argument.

The big earthquake from a couple of weeks ago is still generating news — buildings that shouldn't have collapsed are being investigated, and someone is probably going to be named as the contractor who cut corners. But the oil story is so much bigger right now that the earthquake has become a side note. The main story is money moving fast, companies signing papers, and a country trying to prove it can be fixed before the window of foreign confidence closes.

The week was defined by a wave of international deals, diplomatic engagements, and foreign investor arrivals that signal a new era of Venezuela's reintegration into the global economy.

judged.reading_a: Forecast A is highly structured with six themed predictions and explicit confidence levels. It correctly anticipated the oil investment momentum: Ensign (Canada) announcing drilling rig fleet growth, Qatar's UCC pursuing onshore expansion, and Nabep boosting production all fit A's expectation of a 'seventh or eighth company name' and concrete next-stage commitments. The 'looting' criticism and US-as-manager/creditor framing A predicted align well with Bloomberg's 'zero transparency' coverage, Democrats planning probes of the $100 billion oil deal, and the 'US pulling the strings' narrative. A's prediction that Machado would 'resurface with a specific demand' is a clear hit: she urged a more drastic oil-sector overhaul and questioned the Trump deal while committing to US ties. The Colombia security angle is partially hit by Hegseth's follow-up trip to Colombia to 'hunt and defeat' narcotrafic. A also correctly flagged a second earthquake as a possibility, though it placed it in the 'would not bet on' list and the actual event (strongest quakes in over a century on Nov 20) was far more dramatic than a minor aftershock. However, A overcommitted to several specific predictions that did not materialize: the Vitol-Vance controversy, the IDB loan decision, Petrobras's Caracas trip, Ecopetrol's gas talks, and a concrete power-law implementation step were all expected but absent from the headlines. The power crisis, which A gave medium-high confidence, was not the dominant story. A also missed the two biggest actual stories entirely: the US-Venezuela military partnership (Hegseth's surprise visit and defense pact) and the TPS/migrant deportation saga (appeals court ruling, Supreme Court bid, Jorge Linares detention). The $26.6 billion borrowing bill and the Guyanese territory float were also unanticipated. Overall, A captured the right direction on oil and US-Venezuela dynamics but made too many specific predictions that missed, and its 'would not bet on: a second major earthquake' line is a notable stumble given what actually happened.
judged.reading_b: Forecast B is a flowing narrative rather than a structured list, and its predictions are generally less specific, which both helps and hurts. It correctly anticipated the oil investment wave continuing to build, with 'at least one or two additional energy companies' announcing concrete steps — Ensign, Qatar's UCC, and Nabep all fit. The expectation of foreign investor delegations arriving and new countries announcing formal engagement is hit by Canada's Ensign and Qatar's UCC. B's 'less likely surprises' section is notably more accurate than A's equivalent: the 'small corruption probe into pre-transition oil contracts' aligns with Democrats planning formal probes of the $100 billion deal, and the 'minor secondary earthquake' is directionally correct even though the actual event was the strongest in over a century rather than minor. The Colombia security collaboration producing 'at least one joint operation or a joint press statement' is partially hit by Hegseth's Colombia visit and his narcotrafic pledge. B's overall framing of 'cautious, US-guided economic reopening with incremental progress and manageable friction' is a reasonable summary of the week, even though the military deal pushed things slightly beyond purely economic. B also missed the two dominant stories: the US-Venezuela military partnership and the TPS/migrant crisis. The power crisis, which B expected to remain 'a live political issue,' was not the week's focus. B's 'would not bet on: a formal US military or naval deployment' is technically correct (a partnership agreement is not a deployment), but it is close enough to the actual military deal that a reader might feel the forecast was on the edge of it. B did not overcommit to specific wrong details the way A did (no Vitol-Vance, no Petrobras trip, no Ecopetrol term sheet), so its miss profile is cleaner. The 'thirty-somethings in finance and tech returning' and 'small-business and startup activity' predictions did not clearly surface.
judged.comparison: Both forecasts captured the oil investment momentum correctly and both anticipated a second earthquake as a possibility, though both underestimated its magnitude. Both correctly sensed the US-Venezuela relationship deepening and the US playing a managerial role. Both missed the two biggest actual stories — the Hegseth military deal and the TPS/migrant deportation saga — and both overestimated the prominence of the power crisis. The key differentiator is specificity versus accuracy. Forecast A made many specific predictions (Vitol-Vance controversy, IDB loan decision, Petrobras trip, Ecopetrol term sheet, power-law implementation step, Rodriguez's Brazil trip) that did not materialize, and it explicitly placed 'a second major earthquake' in its 'would not bet on' list, which was a notable miss. Forecast B made fewer specific commitments, so it had fewer things to miss, and its 'less likely surprises' section (corruption probe, secondary earthquake) proved more accurate than A's equivalent. B's overall narrative of cautious US-guided reopening with manageable friction is a fairer description of the actual week than A's more granular (and partially wrong) checklist. A reader given B's forecast would have been less surprised by the week's actual shape, while a reader given A's forecast would have been looking for a Vitol-Vance scandal, an IDB loan announcement, and a Petrobras joint statement that never came. Neither forecast is strong, but B's cleaner miss profile and more accurate 'surprise' section give it a slight edge. VERDICT: B

measurement.happened:
This week in Canada was dominated by a surge of trade and diplomatic activity, with Prime Minister Mark Carney on the move on multiple fronts simultaneously. The single biggest story was the Canada-US trade relationship. Carney announced progress on a trade deal with the United States (Reuters, Nov 14; AP, Nov 14), and US Treasury Secretary Bessent expressed optimism about deals with both Canada and Mexico (Reuters, Nov 13). Canada extended tariff relief on certain US imports (Reuters, Nov 9; Bloomberg, Nov 10), and Carney noted that despite Democrats' sweeping midterm wins, Trump remains central to the trade talks (AP, Nov 12). The Canadian dollar underperformed most G10 currencies amid falling oil prices (Reuters, Nov 9). Carney's ambassador warned that Trump tariffs are driving up costs and threatening US investment in Canada (CNBC, Nov 11). Meanwhile, Carney gave oil companies a tax windfall hoping they would reinvest (Bloomberg, Nov 9).

Carney's Asia tour produced several concrete outcomes. He touted a finalized free-trade agreement with the Philippines (AFP, Nov 14; TV5Monde, Nov 14), raised the topic of Chinese auto manufacturing in talks with Xi, and told the Chinese leader that outsiders should not meddle in Canada's affairs (Reuters, Nov 10; Bloomberg, Nov 10). China's Chery was already preparing a winter-adapted electric SUV for the Canadian market (Bloomberg, Nov 10).

The EU-Canada relationship deepened significantly. The two sides launched a new alliance covering Ukraine support, critical minerals, and AI cooperation, described as a 'new chapter' at a Montreal summit (AFP, Nov 13 and Nov 11; DW, Nov 14 and Nov 12). Deutsche Welle framed this as the US conflict pushing Canada closer to the EU (DW, Nov 14, Nov 12).

The Stellantis-Brampton plant saga escalated sharply. Stellantis sold its idled Brampton, Ontario assembly plant to Canadian defense firm Roshel (Reuters, Nov 9; Bloomberg, Nov 10). Carney called the sale 'unacceptable' (WSJ, Nov 11). Canada threatened to sue Stellantis, with the government saying the automaker owed hundreds of millions in breached commitments (AP, Nov 13; Bloomberg, Nov 13; CNBC, Nov 13). Stellantis offered to repay C$24 million, but Ottawa said that was far short of what was owed (WSJ, Nov 13). Roshel is already in talks with automakers to manufacture civilian vehicles at the plant (Reuters, Nov 10). The fight over Canadian steelworker jobs at Cleveland-Cliffs also made headlines, with the company recalling laid-off workers (WSJ, Nov 13; Al Jazeera, Nov 13).

On the financial and monetary front, the Bank of Canada raised rates to contain an oil-price surge caused by the Iran war (Bloomberg, Nov 11; WSJ, Nov 14). Minutes revealed that uncertainty over rates did not mean inaction (Reuters, Nov 10; Bloomberg, Nov 10). BlackRock and Scotiabank economists were seen as contenders to run the Bank of Canada (Bloomberg, Nov 11). Carney recruited Bridgewater co-CIO Karniol-Tambour to lead Canada's new sovereign wealth fund (Reuters, Nov 9; Bloomberg, Nov 9; WSJ, Nov 9). The Canada Pension Investment Board eyes doubling its hedge fund bets to $160 billion (Bloomberg, Nov 11), while another top pension merged its active equities arm and cut dozens of jobs (Bloomberg, Nov 10). RBC eliminated climate and ESG roles amid a reorganization (Reuters, Nov 12), and RBC also announced an agreement to acquire Yarra Capital Management (FT, Nov 9). Omers' global equities chief departed amid a broader Canadian pension shake-up (Bloomberg, Nov 13).

Canada expanded its sanctions regime. Fresh Russia-related sanctions were announced (Reuters, Nov 9), targeting weapons and crypto (WSJ, Nov 10). Canada reimposed sanctions on 11 Iranian entities for contributing to nuclear activities (Reuters, Nov 10). The decision to block Russian players from entering the World Junior Ice Hockey Championships in Canada generated international friction, with Russia threatening sanctions against Canada and Germany (Reuters, Nov 11; DW, Nov 14; Al Jazeera, Nov 12; AP, Nov 11 and Nov 13).

In energy and industry, Canada invested C$200 million in the Woodfibre LNG project to grow its capacity (Reuters, Nov 13), and an Indonesian billionaire's LNG plant received $140 million from Canada (Bloomberg, Nov 14). S&P's Yergin noted LNG is Canada's little-known economic engine (Bloomberg, Nov 12). In nuclear energy, Turkey and Canada's AtkinsRealis signed a deal for a study on a possible nuclear plant (Reuters, Nov 12; Bloomberg, Nov 12; FT, Nov 12), with Turkey reportedly favoring Canada and South Korea for a new nuclear power deal (Bloomberg, Nov 10). Nunavut's premier asked Canada to lift the Arctic drilling moratorium, though Carney said no decision had been made yet (Reuters, Nov 12 and Nov 10).

In tech and AI, Canada announced it was buying a stake in AI firm Cohere to bolster tech sovereignty (AFP, Nov 11). The Canadian-made indie game 'Paralives' thrived despite gaming sector turmoil (AFP, Nov 13). A VC bet that a Georgian soup factory could anchor Canada's tech rise (Bloomberg, Nov 10).

In health, Pfizer announced it would stop selling Premarin hormone therapy in Canada (Reuters, Nov 12), and Health Canada issued a warning after bacteria were found in unauthorized peptides (Reuters, Nov 12). Tandem Diabetes Care received multiple Health Canada approvals for its t:slim X2 insulin pump (FT, Nov 12).

On the environmental and climate front, the UK, Norway, and Canada launched a $10 billion climate finance initiative (Reuters, Nov 13). El Niño was flagged as a potential driver of winter weather patterns in Canada (BBC, Nov 13).

In politics and public life, Alberta's leader faced backlash after winning a referendum to remain in Canada, suggesting the question had generated significant tension (FT, Nov 9). A grizzly bear attack on a mother and daughter, with four bears linked by DNA and subsequently put down, captured national attention (AP, Nov 10; BBC, Nov 11; DW, Nov 12). A false link between an April 2025 pro-Palestinian rally and Ottawa's Remembrance Day was clarified (AFP, Nov 13). Barrick Mining filed for an IPO of its North American business in New York (Reuters, Nov 11). Canada said a firm that sold Cathie Wood's ETFs had taken money from funds (Bloomberg, Nov 10). An RBC poll found Canadians worried they cannot tell real deals from scams during the holiday shopping season (FT, Nov 13).

delta.motion: Five days separate these two photographs of Canada, and the shift is visible in both scale and direction. The US-Canada trade story grew from a vague 'progress' and a murkier week-end picture into concrete momentum: Carney announced a deal, Treasury Secretary Bessent voiced optimism, and tariff relief on certain US imports was extended. The tone moved from anxious negotiation to something closer to closure. The EU-Canada relationship grew the fastest of any bilateral thread, leaping from 'moving closer toward a formal association' in the first photo to a launched 'new alliance' at a Montreal summit covering Ukraine support, critical minerals, and AI. That is a structural jump in one week. The Bank of Canada moved from a cautious 'proceed carefully' posture to an actual rate hike driven by an oil-price surge tied to the Iran war, a decisive shift in monetary stance. The sovereign wealth fund story around Karniol-Tambour grew from a single hiring announcement into a broader succession conversation, with BlackRock and Scotiabank economists now being named as potential future Bank of Canada governors. Sanctions expanded: the first photo mentioned eight money-services firms hit over Iran; the second adds fresh Russia sanctions targeting weapons and crypto plus eleven Iranian entities tied to nuclear activity. The Asia dimension grew substantially, from China's debut yuan and green bond sales to Carney physically touring the region, finalizing a free-trade agreement with the Philippines, and sitting down with Xi to discuss Chinese auto manufacturing. Energy stories multiplied: the first photo had one Blackstone LNG investment; the second adds C$200 million for Woodfibre LNG, $140 million for an Indonesian plant, a Turkey nuclear study, and a Nunavut push to lift the Arctic drilling moratorium. The World Juniors hockey drama intensified: Russia went from threatening a six-country boycott to threatening sanctions against Canada and Germany, raising the stakes from sports to trade. A major new story appeared that was barely present in the first photo: the Stellantis-Brampton plant sale to defense firm Roshel, Carney calling it 'unacceptable,' and a government threat to sue over hundreds of millions in breached commitments. This industrial-policy fight is now one of the dominant threads. On the shrinking side, the detailed budget line items (housing relaxations, the 200,000 permanent-resident grants, the homelessness fund, the bank ownership reforms) that dominated the first photo have receded into background; the Francophonie summit and the Yellowknife military exercises have largely vanished from the news cycle; the Sherritt furlough, the Foodtastic/MTY bid, and the Starlink rival battle have disappeared; the Canada-India bank takeover, while still ongoing, has dropped out of the headline layer. The grizzly bear attack, which in the first photo was a fresh tragedy sparking policy calls, has resolved into a concrete outcome: four bears linked by DNA and put down. The Alberta referendum backlash persists but has plateaued rather than escalated. In short, the motion is outward and multipolar: Canada is closing deals, launching alliances, raising rates, buying stakes, and threatening lawsuits simultaneously, while the domestic budget mechanics and the cultural-summit stories fade into the background. The center of gravity has shifted from 'what will the budget do' to 'who will we be partners with, and what will we force our own companies to do.'
delta.wind: The expectation was broadly right on the main axis and wrong on several secondary ones. The forecast that US-Canada trade would remain the center of gravity was confirmed and then exceeded: Carney made multiple public statements, Bessent voiced optimism, and tariff relief was extended, all within the week. The expectation that Democratic members of Congress would press the White House was met. The prediction that the Karniol-Tambour appointment would generate follow-up coverage about the fund's mandate was correct, and the story grew into a wider Bank of Canada succession speculation that was not anticipated. The World Juniors drama was expected to continue, and it did, but it escalated beyond the forecast: Russia moved from threatening a boycott to threatening sanctions, a step the expectation only flagged as 'possible.' The Canadian dollar and jobs data staying in the headlines was accurate; the dollar underperformed G10 currencies. The expectation that the Bank of Canada might release a policy note or have a governor speak was met in a stronger form: the Bank actually raised rates, a more decisive action than a reassuring note. The China bond sales and extended tariff deal were expected to produce concrete announcements, and they did, but the story grew into a full Asia tour with a finalized Philippines FTA and a direct Xi meeting, which was not in the forecast. The EU-Canada association talks were expected to get a scheduling update; instead they produced a launched 'new alliance' at a summit, a bigger step than anticipated. The Alberta referendum backlash was expected to generate a few more headlines without a full crisis, and that is exactly what happened. The grizzly bear attack was expected to move into the formal investigation phase with preliminary findings; it resolved more quickly, with the bears identified and put down. The expectation that the Starlink rival battle might see a public filing or regulatory hearing was not strongly met; the story faded. The Canada-India bank takeover committee hearing was not prominently reported. The Francophonie wrap-up was expected to produce a few cultural and defense stories, but it largely vanished from the news cycle. The forecast that the week would be 'busy but incremental' was partly wrong: the Stellantis-Brampton plant sale, with Carney calling it 'unacceptable' and threatening a lawsuit, was a major new industrial-policy confrontation that was not in the first photograph and is not in the expectation. The Bank of Canada rate hike was a more forceful action than the 'proceed carefully' note the expectation anticipated. The Cohere AI stake purchase, the $10 billion climate finance initiative with the UK and Norway, the Pfizer Premarin withdrawal, the Turkey nuclear study, and the Nunavut Arctic drilling question are all stories that appeared without being forecast. The expectation correctly ruled out an early election, a cabinet reshuffle, a constitutional crisis, a major Carney scandal, and a trade-bloc membership change, and none of those happened. The pattern of being wrong is instructive: the expectation under-weighted the speed at which the EU-Canada relationship could move from talks to a launched alliance, under-weighted the Bank of Canada's willingness to hike rather than merely signal, and completely missed the Stellantis-Brampton industrial fight, which emerged as one of the week's defining stories. The expectation also over-weighted the budget implementation details as a news driver; those specifics receded quickly. The broader lesson is that for Canada in this period, the expectation model tends to treat the US trade relationship as a slow negotiation and the domestic policy debates as the main engine, when in reality the country is moving on multiple fronts at once and corporate-industrial confrontations can erupt with little warning and dominate the cycle.
delta.driver: The single force pushing Canada from the first photograph to the second is a government executing a multi-front de-risking strategy against structural dependence on the United States, while the United States remains the dominant economic gravity well. Carney is not just negotiating tariffs; he is simultaneously building alternative trade architecture (the Philippines FTA, the EU alliance, the China engagement, the Turkey nuclear study), reshaping the domestic financial system (the sovereign wealth fund, the Bank of Canada rate hike, pension fund restructuring, the Cohere stake), and asserting industrial policy over corporate freedom (the Stellantis-Brampton fight, the oil tax windfall, the Cleveland-Cliffs steelworker recall). Every thread in the second photograph is a consequence of that same underlying tension: Canada wants to be less dependent, but its largest market, its largest investor, and its most important supply-chain partner are all the United States, and the US is in the middle of a tariff war, a midterm power shift, and its own domestic disputes. The Bank of Canada is caught between an oil-price shock from the Iran war and a weak domestic labor market, forcing it to act rather than wait. The EU-Canada alliance is, as Deutsche Welle framed it, a direct consequence of the US conflict pushing Canada closer to Europe. The Asia tour is a direct consequence of needing alternative buyers for oil, LNG, and manufactured goods. The Stellantis fight is a direct consequence of a government that has decided industrial policy is a sovereign tool, not a private-sector matter. The driver is not one event or one policy; it is the structural mismatch between Canada's economic geography and its political ambition to be less tethered to its neighbor, and every week's news is the friction generated by trying to close that gap while the gap keeps being pulled back open by the size and proximity of the US economy.

judged.reading_a: Forecast A built its week around ten themes, with US-Canada trade formalization as the dominant story. It predicted a joint press conference, signing, or detailed public breakdown of the US-Canada deal, with high confidence this would dominate. In reality, Trump said on November 20 that 'more work' was needed, Bloomberg reported the US was closer to a Mexico deal than to one with Canada, and the US-Canada story ground on without a concrete milestone. The actual dominant trade story was the Canada-China pivot at APEC, which A never named as a theme. It appears only in the 'less likely surprises' list as a possible Chinese EV launch. A's Stellantis prediction of a legal filing or formal government claim was close in spirit but the actual event was Canada offering Stellantis options to keep the Ontario plant open, a negotiation gesture rather than a court filing. A's EU-Canada theme expected a concrete deliverable or working-group meeting; the DW headline 'Conflict with US pushes Canada closer to EU' appeared, but no specific joint document or action dominated coverage. A's World Juniors and Russia sanctions theme was well-calibrated: Russia was formally barred by the IIHF, Moscow threatened an IOC appeal, and Carney publicly called Putin 'lying' about sanctions, matching A's expectation of the 'threaten to do' motion materializing. A's financial system theme correctly anticipated the BoC rate-hike aftermath and succession speculation; in fact, Governor Macklem announced his 2027 departure, kicking off a formal succession race, which A had flagged as a likely coverage driver. A's energy theme was partially right: Ensign's Venezuela drilling expansion and the CNR-Advantage Energy deal hit, and an LNG site story appeared, though the specific Woodfibre and Turkey nuclear updates were not the headlines. A's health theme (Pfizer Premarin, peptide warning) did not surface in the week's headlines. A's Alberta theme correctly predicted a quiet week. A's climate theme was partially validated by the North Star Carbon Removal selection and the $392.5 million Brazil forest fund pledge. What A missed entirely as a major story: the Quebecor-Telus $21.96 billion bid, the government's Cohere stake, the KPMG cyber incident, the fifth soldier's death, the NATO Innovation Fund, the data-center story (Canada as the destination US states reject), the Alphabet $3.5 billion Canadian debt sale, the Tim Hortons-Israeli data deal, Hegseth's military restrictions, and Carney's travel as a story in itself (five continents, 32 countries in 113 days). A's 'what I would not bet on' list was largely accurate: no cabinet reshuffle, no federal election, no full US-Canada signed agreement, no BoC rate-hike reversal. Overall, A painted a week of US-centric trade formalization and a Stellantis legal battle, and the actual week was a China-centric trade pivot with Stellantis in negotiation mode. The direction was partially right, but the center of gravity was wrong.
judged.reading_b: Forecast B led with trade and diplomacy as the center of gravity, noting Carney's Asia tour would likely continue or wind down and that the US trade deal 'progress' language would be the headline. The Asia tour was indeed the vehicle for the week's dominant story: Carney met Xi at APEC, touted the Philippine deal, and fielded questions from Taiwan's foreign minister. measurement.happened:
This week in Iraq was dominated by four intertwined stories, each pulling in a different direction.

The first and loudest theme was oil. Iraq's October crude output jumped to the highest level since 2019, according to the IEA data cited by Bloomberg. That is a big deal in a country where oil revenue funds roughly half the government budget. At the same time, Reuters broke an exclusive that Baghdad is reviving an overland truck route through Syria to ship oil out of the country, a clear sign that Iraq wants to reduce its dependence on the Strait of Hormuz and the Turkish pipeline. CNBC noted that both Saudi Arabia and Iraq are ramping up output as Gulf producers hedge against Hormuz risks. So the picture is one of a country pushing production to record levels while quietly building alternative export corridors. Supporting headlines: Bloomberg (Oct output), Reuters (Syrian truck route), CNBC (Hormuz adaptation).

Closely tied to the oil story was the Khor Mor gas field, one of Iraq's major gas assets, which was forced to halt production after a drone attack, as reported by both Reuters and Al Jazeera. Al Jazeera framed it as raising fears about Iraq's broader energy security. In a country that is already trying to diversify exports, a drone hitting a gas field in the north is a reminder that the energy infrastructure is not just an economic asset but a military target. The operator confirmed the halt, and the timing two days after the output record makes the vulnerability feel more acute.

The second major theme was Iraq's delicate dance with Iran and US sanctions. On November 9, Iraq announced it would reopen the Sheeb border crossing with Iran while temporarily closing the Mandali crossing, a small but symbolic reshuffling of the border landscape. Two days later, Baghdad barred the plane carrying Iran's national soccer team from landing in Basra, citing US sanctions, and the team had to arrive by bus. That story was picked up by Reuters and Al Jazeera (multiple angles). It is a small event in isolation, but it perfectly captures Iraq's position: close enough to Iran to host its national team, yet careful enough to invoke US sanctions to avoid a diplomatic slap. The bus arrival became a minor media moment, a visual of the friction.

The third theme, and arguably the most politically charged, was the killing of former Iraqi MP Ahmed al-Alwani in Beirut. AP reported the killing on November 12, and Al Jazeera followed up the next day with the detail that Lebanon had asked Syria to extradite the suspects. The fact that a former Iraqi lawmaker was found dead in Lebanon, and that the investigation immediately reached across to Syria, turns a single homicide into a three-country political puzzle. For Baghdad, it is an embarrassment and a prompt: who was al-Alwani, what was he doing in Beirut, and why did he have to die? The story will not go away quietly.

A lighter but notable thread ran through the week: Baghdad opened its first Jewish museum, and both Reuters and BBC reported that it was drawing crowds eager to rediscover Iraq's Jewish past. It is a cultural milestone, a small act of national self-reflection in a country that has largely moved on from its pre-1950 Jewish community. It also fits the broader regional trend of soft-power and historical reconciliation projects.

Finally, Al Jazeera noted that Iran was holding a ceremony honouring fallen soldiers from the Iran-Iraq War, complete with a missile display. The war ended in 1988, so this is well past the 40th anniversary, but the ritual of commemoration with hardware on show keeps the old rivalry alive in the public imagination, even as the two neighbours trade oil, players, and border crossings.

Taken together, the week paints a picture of a country that is economically confident (record oil output), diplomatically juggling (sanctions, borders, Syria), politically bruised (the Alwani killing), culturally curious (the museum), and still haunted by its wars (the missile ceremony).
measurement.expected:
Looking at the week ahead, November 14 through roughly November 21, I would frame my expectations around the same themes, with a few additions.

Oil and the Syrian truck route: I am almost certain this will remain a top story. The Reuters exclusive is fresh, and the logistics of moving Iraqi crude by truck through Syria are complex, politically sensitive, and expensive to set up. Expect follow-up reporting on the volume of trucks, the condition of the road, the fees Syria charges, and whether the route is a one-off or a structural shift. I am also probable that the Khor Mor halt will be extended or that a second site will be hit, because the drone attack signals that whoever struck it (and we do not yet know for sure whether it was a Turkish, Kurdish, or Iranian-linked actor) sees the energy infrastructure as a bargaining chip. A full restart of Khor Mor within the week is possible but I would not bet on it without a visible security upgrade.

The Alwani killing: I am probable that this will generate at least one more round of political drama. Baghdad will likely issue a statement or open a formal investigation, and the Lebanese-Syrian extradition request will either move forward or stall, generating headlines in all three capitals. There is a possible, though not certain, chance that Iraqi parliamentarians will call an ad-hoc session or demand a briefing from the foreign ministry. I would rate a full-blown cabinet reshuffle or a formal note of protest to Lebanon as unlikely within this short window, but a pointed press conference from the Iraqi foreign ministry is probable. The question of who al-Alwani was and what he was doing in Beirut will keep the story alive.

Iran border and sanctions: I am almost certain the Sheeb reopening and Mandali closure will be implemented on the ground, with trucks and passengers flowing through the new crossing. I am probable that at least one more small sanctions-related friction will surface, perhaps a cargo plane or a diplomatic convoy, because the soccer-team incident showed that the rules are being applied selectively and both sides are testing the boundaries. A full diplomatic spat is unlikely; Iraq needs Iran and does not want to offend Washington.

The Jewish museum: I am almost certain it will continue to generate cultural and social-media coverage, and I am probable that at least one Israeli or Western diplomat will visit or send a congratulatory note, which will in turn trigger a small domestic debate in Baghdad about the symbolism. A political crisis over the museum is unlikely.

Iran-Iraq war commemoration: The missile-display ceremony is a recurring annual event, so I am almost certain it will not reappear within the week unless a new provocation triggers it. But I am possible that Iraqi media will run retrospective pieces or that a local militia will issue a statement tying the old war to the present, especially if the Khor Mor attack is attributed to an Iranian-linked group.

Things I would not bet on in the next week: a full-scale military clash between Iraq and a neighbour (the drone attack is a probe, not a war); a snap parliamentary election triggered by the Alwani killing; a new oil-for-roads mega-deal with Syria announced before the logistics are even working; a government resignation or cabinet reshuffle; or a second major drone attack on a different energy site before the first one is even investigated.

Less likely but possible surprises: a formal US sanctions waiver or carve-out for the Syrian truck route, which would be a small but significant diplomatic signal; a surprise visit by an Iraqi energy minister to Damascus or Tehran to finalize the overland deal; a parliamentary vote of no confidence in the foreign minister over the Alwani handling; a second drone strike, this time on a pipeline or a refinery, to ratchet up pressure; or the museum becoming a flashpoint for a small protest by a conservative or Shia bloc that questions the timing of celebrating a pre-Islamic community.

Overall, I expect a week of managed tension: oil flowing, borders shifting, one assassination echoing, a museum drawing crowds, and a drone scar slowly healing. No war, no revolution, but enough moving parts to keep the news cycle busy.

The story did not explode into a vote of no confidence or a snap election; it simply lost its headline dominance to the oil record and the Alwani killing. The expectation was partly right that the crisis would not be neatly resolved, but wrong that it would remain the central story. It was more of a slow bleed than a dramatic rupture, and other news overtook it. On energy, the expectation that Khor Mor would remain offline through the end of the week came true; the field is still halted. The expectation of repeated blackouts and federal government intervention was probably correct in practice but did not generate a distinct headline in the second photograph. The possibility of a second drone strike did not materialise in this window. The expectation of a visible, phased closure of border crossings with Iran came true in a slightly different form: rather than a broad shutdown, Iraq reopened Sheeb and closed Mandali, a targeted swap that fits the 'phased and targeted' language the forecast predicted. The soccer-team-bus story is a perfect, if small, illustration of the sanctions juggling that the forecast anticipated. The expectation that al-Zaidi or another senior official would make at least one more high-profile contact with Washington or Tehran was probably met in back channels, but no specific new contact is named in the second photograph. The Hormuz oil-export terms were not publicly announced in this window, so that specific expectation did not come to fruition. The federal-cabinet emergency session and PM public address were predicted as probable but do not appear as distinct headlines in the second photograph, though the Alwani killing would likely trigger such a session in the coming days. The expectation of street protests or a sit-in in Erbil or Sulaymaniyah over the blackouts did not materialise in the headlines, though the Khor Mor halt is still ongoing and the anger is presumably building below the surface. The less-likely surprises on the radar (snap election, corruption scandal, flash flood, second drone wave, US airstrike) did not appear. What was not expected and did appear: the record oil output and the Syrian overland truck route, which reframed the energy story from a crisis narrative to a growth-and-diversification narrative. The Alwani killing in Beirut was a genuine surprise, pulling in Lebanon and Syria and adding a security-and-investigation dimension that the first photograph did not contain. The Jewish museum opening was a small cultural beat that the forecast did not anticipate. The Iran-Iraq War ceremony with a missile display is a minor but telling reminder that the old rivalry still has a public ritual, even as the two countries trade oil and bus-ride soccer teams. Overall, the forecast over-weighted the Kurdish internal politics as the dominant story and under-weighted the oil economics as a standalone headline. It correctly captured the border-diplomacy trajectory and the Khor Mor downtime but missed the Beirut thread entirely and did not anticipate that Iraq's economic confidence (record output, new routes) would become as prominent as its diplomatic juggling. The 'sandwich' framing was directionally right, but the specific stories playing out in week two were more about Iraq asserting economic agency and dealing with a cross-border homicide than about the Kurdish cabinet breaking or the border closing wholesale.
delta.driver: The force pushing Iraq from the first photograph to the second is, at its core, a country trying to convert economic momentum into diplomatic leverage while absorbing a new political shock from the Levant. Record oil output and the decision to build a Syrian overland export route are not just economic decisions; they are statements of independence, a way for Baghdad to say it can feed its budget and ship its barrels without fully depending on either the Turkish pipeline or the Strait of Hormuz, and therefore without fully depending on either Washington or Tehran. That economic confidence gives Baghdad room to be more granular and less dramatic in its border diplomacy, reopening Sheeb while closing Mandali, letting Iran's soccer team in by bus, and keeping the Hormuz exemption without needing to announce grand trilateral frameworks. At the same time, the Khor Mor drone hit is a reminder that the energy infrastructure that underpins that confidence is a military target, and the Alwani killing in Beirut is a reminder that Iraq's political class is still entangled in the Levantine web of alliances, grudges, and cross-border investigations. The Kurdish cabinet crisis, while real, is being absorbed into a broader narrative of national economic assertion and external juggling, so it loses headline space. The underlying driver is therefore Iraq's attempt to be a more economically self-sufficient and diplomatically autonomous player in a US-Iran standoff, while managing the internal and regional frictions (Kurdish politics, the Beirut homicide, the old Iran-Iraq rivalry) that threaten to pull it back into the middle.

crystal.reasoning:
Starting from the present: Iraq enters this week with record oil output, a newly revived Syrian overland truck route, a gas field still dark after a drone hit, a former MP dead in Beirut with the investigation reaching into Syria, a soccer team that had to ride a bus because of US sanctions, and a brand-new Jewish museum drawing crowds. The wind tells me I over-weighted Kurdish politics last time, under-weighted oil as a standalone headline, missed the Beirut thread entirely, and that Iraq's stories shift faster than I expect while structural fragility is consistently underestimated.

The wind correction: last time I missed a cross-border thread entirely, so I am weighting this more heavily now.

I expect logistics details, a possible government press conference on the route's capacity and timeline, and continued OPEC-plus commentary as both Iraq and Saudi Arabia push output. I expect a repair timeline announcement, possibly a Kurdish government demand for federal compensation, and a small but real chance of a second drone strike on energy infrastructure. The wind correction: I under-weighted oil last time, so I am giving it more space. The Khor Mor gas field will still be offline, and I expect a repair timeline to be published, along with a Kurdish government demand for federal compensation for the ongoing blackout. There is a meaningful probability, perhaps one in four, of a second drone strike on energy infrastructure in the north, because the field has now been proven as a target and the economic stakes of the record-output narrative make the infrastructure more visible. Border micro-diplomacy with Iran will continue in small, granular ways. I expect one or two more sanctions-juggling moments: a denied flight, a held truck, a minor adjustment to crossing hours at Sheeb. The overall posture will remain 'open but managed.' I would not expect a full closure or a grand new framework. Confidence: high for the continuation of the pattern; medium for any single specific event.

The PUK-KDP coalition tension is real but is being absorbed into the broader national narrative of economic assertion and the Beirut investigation. I expect at most one quiet ministerial reshuffle or a back-channel reconciliation, not a public rupture. The wind correction from last week tells me I should not let this story consume the forecast. Confidence: medium-high that it stays in the background.

The Jewish museum will generate a few more follow-up pieces, possibly a small diplomatic or cultural event tied to it, and the Iran-Iraq War ceremony will fade from the news cycle within two days. These are color, not story. Confidence: high that they are minor.

The Alwani killing is the power-and-deaths story this week; a second one would be too coincidental.

crystal.eli5:
Iraq had a big week: they pumped more oil than they have in years, and they are building a new road through Syria to ship that oil to the sea instead of relying on one narrow waterway. But then a drone hit a gas field up north, and the lights went out for a lot of people. On top of that, a former politician was found dead in Lebanon, and now three countries are trying to figure out who did it and why.

Next week, the main story will probably be the politician's death. The Iraqi government will hold a meeting, make statements, and start asking hard questions. Lebanon and Syria are already involved in the investigation, so this is not just an Iraqi problem anymore. Think of it like a mystery where the clue leads to three different houses, and the neighbors are all arguing about whose fault it is.

The oil story will keep growing. Iraq will probably announce details about the new truck route through Syria, like how many trucks it can handle and when it will open. The gas field that was hit by the drone will still be broken, and the Kurdish government will be pushing the federal government to pay for the power outage. There is a real chance another drone could show up, because the gas field has now been proven to be a target.

The border with Iran is in a weird middle state. One crossing is open, another is closed, and Iran's soccer team had to ride a bus into the country because of US sanctions rules. That kind of small, awkward juggling will probably continue, but nothing dramatic is expected. The internal politics in the Kurdish north are still tense, but they are being pushed to the back of the news by the bigger stories.

The lighter note: Baghdad just opened its first Jewish museum, and people are going. It is a small, proud moment for a country remembering a community it lost decades ago. And Iran held a ceremony honoring soldiers from the old war with Iraq, complete with a missile display, which is a reminder that even when two neighbors are trading oil and soccer players, the old scars are still there.

judged.reading_a: Forecast A framed the week as one of 'managed tension' across several parallel threads: oil logistics (especially the Syrian truck route and Khor Mor), the Alwani assassination reverberating through Baghdad-Beirut-Damascus, small Iran-border frictions, the Jewish museum drawing cultural attention, and the Iran-Iraq War commemoration fading. It explicitly listed what it would not bet on, including a full-scale military clash, a snap election, a cabinet reshuffle, and a second major drone strike. In practice, the week's dominant story was the Jurf al-Sakhar standoff with Kataib Hezbollah, in which the PM sacked nine officials over oil smuggling, the army deployed, an IRGC commander flew in for talks, and a compromise was reached. Neither A nor B named this confrontation. A's oil/energy theme was directionally correct: the week saw the resumption of the Turkey pipeline, a drone alarm at an Iraqi gas field, tankers hit in the Strait of Hormuz, and a deadly Basra power-station fire. A's 'drone scar slowly healing' was undercut by the new drone alarm, but the broader energy-fragility theme landed. A's treatment of Alwani as 'probable to generate at least one more round of political drama' was more measured than B's and closer to reality, since the killing stayed in the background rather than dominating. A's 'almost certain' that the Sheeb/Mandali border adjustments would be implemented on the ground is plausible but not clearly reflected in the headlines. The museum and war-commemoration items were indeed minor, as A predicted. A's 'less likely but possible surprises' list included a surprise visit by an Iraqi energy minister to Damascus or Tehran; the PM actually visited Lebanon to explore oil routes beyond Hormuz, which is in the same neighborhood. A's overall picture of 'no war, no revolution, but enough moving parts' is a fair description of a week that ended in a negotiated compromise rather than a shooting war. A missed the Basra fire, the Telegram block, the French-national sentencing, and the border earthquake, none of which were flagged. The militia standoff, the week's clear lead story, was absent from A's framework entirely, though A's 'managed tension' language and its prediction of no full-scale clash are consistent with how that story actually played out.
judged.reading_b: Forecast B placed the Alwani killing as 'the most likely dominant story of next week' with high confidence, which turned out to be an overstatement: the killing generated some coverage but was clearly secondary to the Jurf al-Sakhar confrontation. B's oil-and-energy section was well calibrated. It expected a government announcement with specific numbers on the Syrian overland route, a Khor Mor repair timeline, and a Kurdish demand for compensation; the actual oil story was somewhat different (Turkey pipeline resumption, Hormuz tanker hits, PM's Lebanon trip), but the broad theme of energy expansion and infrastructure fragility was right. B's 'one in four' probability for a second drone strike on energy infrastructure was a notable calibrated hit, since a drone did raise alarm at an Iraqi gas field on November 17. B's 'open but managed' characterization of the Iran border was accurate, and the IRGC commander's visit to Iraq fits that pattern. B correctly predicted that Kurdish internal politics would stay in the background, that the museum and war ceremony would be minor, and that none of its 'would not bet on' items (snap Kurdistan election, US airstrike, full border closure, second Levantine killing, flash flood, major corruption scandal) materialized. B missed the Jurf al-Sakhar standoff, the Basra power-station fire, the Telegram block, the French-national sentencing, and the earthquake. The oil-smuggling angle that triggered the militia confrontation is adjacent to B's oil narrative but was not the same story. B's over-confidence in Alwani as the week's lead is its most visible miscalibration. Otherwise, B's structure of one dominant political story plus an expanding energy narrative plus managed border micro-diplomacy is a reasonable skeleton, even if the identity of the dominant political story was wrong.
judged.comparison: Both forecasts missed the week's actual dominant story: the Jurf al-Sakhar standoff with Kataib Hezbollah, the PM's sacking of nine officials, the army deployment, the IRGC mediator visit, and the negotiated compromise. This is the single biggest gap in both. Both also missed the Basra power-station fire, the simultaneous Telegram block with Jordan, the sentencing of six French nationals to life in prison, and the border earthquake. On the other hand, both correctly identified oil and energy as a major theme, both correctly expected no full-scale war or snap election, and both correctly downplayed the museum and war-commemoration items. The key differentiator is calibration. Forecast A treated the Alwani killing as one of several parallel threads, 'probable to generate at least one more round of political drama,' which is closer to how it actually played out as a background story. Forecast B declared it 'the most likely dominant story' with 'high' confidence, a more conspicuous miss. A's overall framing of 'managed tension, no war, no revolution, enough moving parts' is a better fit for a week that ended in a negotiated compromise with a militia rather than an assassination-driven political crisis. B's specific 'one in four' probability for a second drone strike at energy infrastructure is a well-calibrated hit that A did not match with a specific probability. A's 'surprise visit by an Iraqi energy minister to a Levantine country' is in the same neighborhood as the PM's Lebanon trip, a small but real hit that B did not flag. A's 'things I would not bet on' list is broader and mostly correct. B's is shorter but also mostly correct. Neither forecast is clearly superior; both captured the broad themes (oil, managed Iran relations, no war) and both missed the specific dominant event. A's more balanced multi-thread structure and more measured confidence levels give it a slight edge in serving a reader who would want a realistic picture of a week of 'managed tension' rather than a single-story narrative. But the gap is small.

measurement.happened: This week in Saudi Arabia was dominated by one overwhelming story: a sharp escalation of Houthi missile and drone attacks on the Kingdom, hitting multiple locations and critical infrastructure. The Houthis struck the East-West oil pipeline in the Medina region on November 9 (confirmed by Reuters, FT, and Al Jazeera), then hit a pumping station on the same pipeline on November 12 (Reuters). On November 10, the Saudi-led coalition shot down Houthi missiles aimed at Riyadh (Reuters), and a Saudi official inspected the Aramco office in Riyadh after a Houthi attack (Reuters). On November 13, the Houthis fired missiles at Saudi forces in Jazan (Reuters), and on November 14 they claimed an attack on the Riyadh financial district, saying the Aramco skyscraper was damaged (AFP). Debris from intercepted missiles fell in the Mecca region on November 12 (Reuters), and on November 11 Saudi Arabia intercepted Houthi missiles and drones while the Houthis denied targeting Mecca (Reuters). A report on November 13 said Saudi Arabia was probing how Houthi missiles had breached its air defenses (Deutsche Welle). Al Jazeera reported on November 10 that attacks were escalating between Saudi-led forces and the Iran-backed Houthis, and on November 13 the Houthis renewed strikes as the UN Security Council extended sanctions. Syria confirmed on November 9 that it was sending troops to Saudi Arabia amid the battle against the Houthis (Al Jazeera, reported twice). Saudi Arabia also pushed the EU to label the Houthis a terrorist group (Reuters, November 12), and Al Gore publicly blasted what he called the 'insane' Saudi veto power at climate talks (AFP and TV5Monde, November 13). In Sanaa, Yemen, there was a tribute to dozens of victims of strikes attributed to Saudi Arabia (TV5Monde, November 11). The oil and energy sector felt the shock directly. Oil settled three dollars higher on the attacks on Saudi energy sites and Strait of Hormuz disruptions (Reuters, November 12). The East-West pipeline was struck in the Medina region (FT, November 9). Saudi oil output surged to one of its highest levels in years (Bloomberg, November 11), and OPEC+ output in October neared pre-Iran war rates, led by Saudi Arabia (Reuters, November 11; WSJ, November 11; FT, November 11). A Saudi oil tanker crossed the Strait of Hormuz with US coordination (Bloomberg, November 10), and the UAE was selling Saudi oil from a supertanker attacked in the Gulf (Reuters, November 10). CNBC noted on November 12 that Saudi and Iraqi oil output were surging as Gulf producers adapted to Hormuz risks. On the financial and economic front, Saudi Arabia postponed its major FII event to October 2027 as Houthi strikes continued (Reuters, November 12; Bloomberg, November 12). The Public Investment Fund was weighing fresh fundraising options to generate cash from its portfolio companies (Reuters, November 10). Bloomberg reported on November 11 that a Saudi liquidity squeeze was adding to challenges for the Crown Prince. Goldman Sachs and Fortress backed a rare Saudi Arabia private credit deal (Bloomberg, November 12). Pakistan and Saudi investors launched a joint fund to boost trade and investment (Reuters, November 9). Lucid missed Wall Street earnings expectations and expanded a loan from a Saudi fund (CNBC, November 9). On the diplomatic and international stage, Saudi Arabia and Turkey signed a deal to build 3,000 megawatts of wind power capacity (Reuters, November 11). The United States signed a participation contract for Expo 2030 Riyadh (AFP, November 11). Trump told Reuters on November 9 that Qatar and Saudi Arabia wanted a peaceful Iran deal, with the US ready for strikes if needed. In the military and defense space, Saudi Arabia's The Helicopter Company ordered 12 Bombardier jets in a fixed-wing aviation push (Reuters, November 13). In sports and entertainment, Formula E rescheduled its Saudi Arabian season opener due to the conflict (Reuters, November 12). The Six Kings Slam tennis tournament was postponed (Deutsche Welle, November 13). Riyadh Season hosted Zuffa Boxing with McKenna defending a world title (BBC, November 14). Saudi Pro League matches were played as normal (BBC, multiple dates). Jannik Sinner planned a late-December return at a Saudi exhibition ahead of the Australian Open (AP, November 10). On the human rights and justice front, TV5Monde reported on November 12 that 520 Ethiopians condemned to death for drug trafficking in Saudi Arabia were awaiting execution. In the corporate and industrial sphere, several Saudi company profiles appeared in Bloomberg and Reuters (Saudi Cement, Saudi Ceramics, Saudi Real Estate, Yamama Cement), and Saudi Arabia's Wall Street hub became a target of Houthi strikes (Bloomberg, November 9).

The pattern this week shows repeated attacks on the East-West pipeline, Riyadh, Jazan, and the Mecca region, and the Houthis have shown no sign of slowing down. The Saudi government will likely announce further interceptions, and there is a probable chance of at least one new attack on either the pipeline or a city in the western or southern regions. The air defense probe reported on November 13 (Deutsche Welle) will likely produce a public statement or a small-scale review announcement, but a full public disclosure of the breach details is possible rather than certain. Syria's troops on Saudi soil (Al Jazeera, November 9) will likely remain a quiet background factor; a public confirmation of their role or a joint Saudi-Syrian military statement is possible but not the main expectation. Saudi oil output will likely stay near its current elevated levels as the Kingdom compensates for pipeline disruptions by ramping up other export routes. A new strike on the East-West pipeline or another Gulf shipping incident is probable. The PIF fundraising options (Reuters, November 10) and the liquidity squeeze (Bloomberg, November 11) will likely generate more analyst commentary and possibly a small market reaction, but no dramatic policy shift is expected within a single week. The Goldman-Fortress private credit deal (Bloomberg, November 12) may see a closing announcement or a follow-up press release, which is possible. Diplomacy and international relations: Saudi Arabia's push to get the EU to designate the Houthis as a terrorist group (Reuters, November 12) will likely see continued diplomatic activity, with a possible EU statement or vote in the coming days. The Saudi-Turkey wind power deal (Reuters, November 11) is already signed, so the next step is likely a technical or implementation announcement, which is possible. The UN Security Council sanctions extension (Al Jazeera, November 13) will likely be followed by a Saudi diplomatic reaction or a statement from the Saudi UN mission. The Al Gore climate veto criticism (AFP, TV5Monde, November 13) will likely generate a Saudi foreign ministry or climate ministry response, which is probable. A new rescheduling announcement or a revised date for one of these events is probable. The Saudi Pro League will continue its regular schedule (BBC, multiple dates), so match reports and results are almost certain. The Zuffa Boxing event at Riyadh Season (BBC, November 14) will likely generate post-fight coverage and possibly an announcement of the next Riyadh Season event, which is possible. A full commutation or execution announcement within a single week is unlikely. The Saudi-led coalition's operational tempo against the Houthis will likely continue, with probable reports of further shoot-downs or ground operations. Less likely surprises: A sudden Houthi ceasefire proposal or a Saudi-Houthi back-channel negotiation leak; a major Saudi cabinet reshuffle triggered by the crisis; a new Saudi nuclear or space announcement; a dramatic PIF portfolio sale or buyout; a Saudi-Iran direct summit. delta.motion:
The dominant theme between the two photographs is the Houthi attack cycle, and it grew sharply. On November 9 the kingdom had just absorbed the Aramco skyscraper hit and the first East-West pipeline strike. By November 14 the pipeline had been hit a second time at a pumping station, missiles had been fired at Jazan, debris from intercepted weapons had fallen in the Mecca region, and the Houthis had re-claimed the Aramco tower as a target. The number of distinct strike events roughly doubled, and the geographic spread widened from Riyadh and the Medina corridor to Jazan and the Mecca area. The bond market was under parallel stress: Bloomberg reported Japan 30-year bond yields jumped tracking a US Treasury selloff, the 30-year bond sale saw weaker demand than the 12-month average, and Japanese savers went on a record government bond spree (FT). Berkshire even tested wider yen spreads in a bond deal, per Bloomberg. All of this feeds into the BOJ debate: the October meeting summary (Reuters, FT) revealed the bank debated the need for faster rate hikes, wholesale inflation accelerated (Reuters), and advisers urged the BOJ to focus on sustaining growth now that inflation has hit its target. The rate question has shifted from whether to hike to the pace and timing of future hikes.

In sports, the week was defined by a humbling 78-15 rugby defeat to England in the Nations Championship, with Will Joseph scoring five tries (BBC, AFP, AP, TV5Monde all covered it). The loss was so lopsided that it overshadowed the fact that Japan's football team had just beaten Brazil 3-2 in Singapore with an injury-time winner (AP, AFP). Tennis fans saw Fernandez reach the Tokyo final while Eala exited. The rugby result also triggered a leadership shakeup: Japan's football boss Moriyasu announced he will leave his position early after the Asian Cup schedule shift (AFP), and rugby coach Jones had vowed before the match that Japan would 'play the house down' against England (AFP) -- a promise that ended up looking bleak.

On the defense and diplomacy front, Reuters broke the exclusive that Japan is warning arms suppliers of deep cuts to expected orders due to a budget squeeze. Japan also agreed to provide coastal radar and drones to the Philippines under a 27 million dollar deal (AP). Takaichi is heading to China for the APEC summit amid degraded relations (TV5Monde), and Japan and Vietnam are eyeing deeper economic security ties following Prime Minister To Lam's visit to Tokyo (Bloomberg). Meanwhile, Japan's dreams of better Russian ties have 'gone up in smoke' (Bloomberg), and Russia's grab of Japan Tobacco was flagged as a risk to Takaichi's spending plan. The industry minister aimed to advance Asia's energy resilience at the AZEC summit (Reuters), and Japan watches for signs of change in Trump's foreign policy after the US midterms (DW).

In corporate news, SoftBank Group sank into losses as its AI hopes faltered (AP), while Nissan reduced its losses and vowed a return to full-year profit (AP). Eneos raised its FY26 net profit forecast 48 percent on stronger oil prices (Reuters). Rapidus is reportedly likely to miss its mass production deadline for chips (Bloomberg), even as Japan manufacturers' mood hit a five-year high on chip demand (Reuters). Toyota is bringing back the Scion brand with Japan's tiny minitrucks to America (WSJ, FT), and a top electronics chain is reportedly eyeing a 630 million dollar store sale (Bloomberg). Anthropic is aiming for a 3 to 3.5 billion dollar offering in Japan (Bloomberg), and Rakuten partnered with AST SpaceMobile on a satellite communications network (FT). The Hello Kitty firm apologized and scrapped a Japan TV tie-up after anger in China (AFP). A Japanese billionaire's complaint against Meta was rejected (TV5Monde). Household spending slumped the most since the pandemic (Bloomberg), while Tokyo's housing boom spread to previously overlooked neighborhoods (Bloomberg).

Other notable items: Japan confirmed its first bird flu case of the season in Kyoto and plans to cull 200,000 birds (Reuters). Cyberattacks hit a third of Japanese firms or their service providers this year (Reuters). Godzilla Minus Zero topped the box office in a win for Japanese cinema (Bloomberg, FT). Quantinuum and RIKEN expanded their quantum-AI supercomputing partnership (FT). Japan's AI robots are preparing for life on the Moon (CNN). FamilyMart's striped socks kept it ahead in the convenience store wars (Reuters).
